LONDON, Sept. 5.-The British
said they were keeping track today
Of the movements of two more ships
believed headed for Palestine with
unauthorized Jewish immigrants.
| A Foreign Office spokesman last
night identified the steamers as the
Northland, heading eastward along
North Africa, and the Paducah, un-
derstood to be at Varna, Bulgaria,
in the Black Sea


He said the vessels, carrying crews
of English speaking Jews with
United States passports, had sailed
from Bayonne, France, the North
land August % and the Paducah
earlier.


The spokesman said the Foreign
Office had failed this week in an
other effort to get France to take
some 4,400 European Jewish refugees
turned back from Palestine in mid
July and now headed for Hamburg.
Germany, aboard three British
transports. They are due in Ham
burg Sunday.


The Foreign Office, he reported.
asked the French government in
formally to let the British land the
Jews in Northern France, but the
French answered that no facilities
were available there for proper care
of the refugees.


Before deciding to intern the Jews
near Hamburg, the British had
sought to disembark them at Port
de Bouc, France, but they had re-
fused to leave the ships, though
French officials at that time had
said they would be welcome.


The group had sailed for Palestine
from Sete, France, aboard the ref
ugee ship Exodus 1947.

FOREST HILLS. N. Y, Aug. 3d.
The high hopes of Australia's Davis
Cuppers went smash again today,
and the huge international tennis
trophy appeared to be safely slowed
away in the land of it's origin for
at least another year after the two
Californians. Jack Kramer and Ted
Schroeder. battered their way to
victory in the opening singles
matches.


Kramer opened the flood gates
with crushing 60, 81, 6-2 win
over curly-haired Dinny Pals, the
Australian champion, and Schroeder
then came through with the second
half of Uncle Sans famous one-two
punch as he charged the net off and
on for more than two hours and
humbled Jack Bromwich, 6-4, 81,
6-3, Ga.


The results thus were duplicate
of the first days play at Melbourne
last December, when the American
pair brought back the cup after it
had been in Australia for seven
years. The only difference was that
Big Jake and the tireless Ted did it
easier this time.


Pals Overwhelmed.


Kramer, the greatest amateur in
the world by far today, simply over
Whelmed Pals. It never was a con-
test from the moment Kramer I'M
limbered his terrific all-court game.
Pals scored only nine placements
in the entire match, and it was
mercifully over after only So min
utes.


Schroeder, to the surprise Of the
experts, made easier work of Brom-
wich than he did eight months ago,
when the Aussie star carried him
the limit of five sets. Except for the
second set. Ted gave the impress
sion all the way that he was play
ing within himself and would win
any point, or half dozen points,
that he deemed necessary.


Ted's service was vastly superior
to Bromwich's soft delivery, and
this made a vital difference in the
games that might have been called
crucial. When he really needed to
hold his service, he did it. In the
third set, where Schroeder went
ahead to stay, he blazed across six
aces and virtually handcuffed
Bromwich with as many other
scorchers.


Bromwich scored only one serv-
ice ace in the entire match. Mostly
he just put the ball in play. This
glaring handicap, coupled with his
complete inability for long stages
to keep Schroeder away from the
net, made his cause hopeless.


Good Spectator Match.


In each of the last two sets
Schroeder bestirred himself to break
through Bromwich's delivery early
and then simply banged his own
across until he had run up the
necessary six games. There were
many long, exciting rallies and it
was a good spectator match, but
Schroeder never gave his followers
any cause for worry.


Five games from the end, Ted
smashed one away at the net with
particular gusto and sprang a pain
full cramp in his racket hand. He
appeared very unhappy, but it did
not affect his game markedly.


Between games a masseur busted
out from under the stands and gave
the hand a brisk rubbing. A mem
Der of the Australian squad pointed
out afterWard that this was some
what irregular. but there was no
protest.


Schroeder expressed confidence
that the effects of the cramp would
not bother him In tomorrow's doubles
match, in which he and Kramer
were scheduled to meet Bromwich
and Colin Long. The odds appeared
long tonight that the two Cali
fornia buddies would win the re-
quired third point tomorrow and
relegate Mondays concluding singles
matches to the exhibition tent.

NEW YORK, Mar. 22.--Individual
stocks continued to make some
headway, in today's market although
quick profit cashing by professional
traders on the weeks rally restrained
many leaders.


Dealings were slow from the start
of the short session. Early advances
OF fractions to q point or so failed
to hold IN most cases and the direc-
ton was somewhat foggy near the
close. Small fractional variations

There were hints today that the
CIO Furniture Workers Union Is
planning some step soon designed
to regain its legal status before the
National Labor Relations Board.


The union was among those whose
officers ignored the October 81 dead
line for submitting nom Communist
affidavits under terms of the Taft
Hartley Act. The NLRB already
has thrown out two of the unions
bargaining election cases.


The Furniture Workers Union is
comparatively small, and the inabil-
ity to use the boards facilities could
be critical in election disputes in
volving other unions which have
complied with the act. The Furni-
ture Workers immediate rival is the
AFL Upholsterers' Union.


Two courses are open to tht
furniture workers $4,000 members
in New York, New England, Penn
sylvania, the South and Midwest


They could:


l. Institute an immediate court
test of the boards right to dismiss
the two cases, thus attacking con.
stitutionality of the anti-Communist
oath and possibly the entire Taft
Hartley Act.


2. Capitulate by either submit
ting affidavits signed by Morris
Pizer, president; Max Perlow, Sec
retary- treasurer, and other officers
or replacing these officers with ones
who will sign.

BRUSSELS, Feb. 27.-Hospital
authorities said today that 40 per-
sons hurt in a riot near the Par
Lament Building yesterday had been
discharged before midnight and only
one policeman still was hospital
lied.


The riot occurred when approx
mately $4,000 demonstrators, de-
manding full payment Of q bonus
for persons imprisoned or deported
by the Nazis, were confronted by
gendarmes and cavalrymen on their
way to the Parliament Building,
where the cabinet was meeting.


The crowd swept through three
lines of these forces and stopped
only when machine guns and rifles
were fired over their heads from
behind steel fencing. The Min
istry Of the Interior said about 40
were injured and one man was
found dead in the street, evidently
Of heart trouble.


1t. Col. Raoul oe F'raiteur, Min
lister of Defense and special tar
get Of the demonstrators slogans,
said the government had not paid
the rest Of the bonus because it did
not have the money.


The gates in front Of Parliament
were broken and litter lay strewn
over surrounding streets today.

With a potential. jurisdictional
dispute simmering in the Senate,
Congress gave signs today of
proceeding slowly with President
Truman's Army-Navy merger
bill.


The measure-patterned after the
compromise program announced by
the White House last month
reached Capitol Hill yesterday and
promptly brought into the open the
long threatened argument over
which Senate committee should
handle it.


While acknowledging there is
plenty Of room for argument, Sen
ate President Vandenberg offered
his opinion that the legislation
should 60 to the Armed Services
Committee headed by Senator Cur
ney.


Final Decision Delayed.


But Chairman Aiken Of the Ex-
penditures Committee protested that
the Is members Of his group had
decided unanimously two weeks ago
they should handle the bill under
terms of the Congressional Reor-
ganization Act.


Before any fireworks could flare,
however. Senator Aiken persuaded
both Senators Vandenberg and
Gurney to delay a final decision un-
til the current argument over budget
cutting is decided-probably tomor-
row.


The House agreed without dispute
to send the measure to its Expendi-
lures Committee, which considered
similar legislation last session with
out action.


Chairman Hoffman indicated his
group will not rush hearings on the
merger proposal, however, because
1t has many other matters Of higher
priority to act on.


Making Five Inquiries Now.


The House committee Is conduct
ing five separate investigations on
topics ranging from surplus prop
erty disposal methods to what Gov
ernment agencies could be abol-
ished.


In the Senate, Senator Gurney
and fellow members of his Armed
Services Committee predicted con-
fidently to a reporter that they will
win Jurisdiction over the measure.


Senator Aiken already had sched-
uled meeting Of his Expenditures
Committee today, and the issue ap-
peared to be likely topic of dis
cusSion.

LAHORE, India, Aug. 14.-Wide
sections of this Punjab capital
were at1ame today in communal
strife which since dawn yester-
day has killed 153 persons by re-
liable unofficial count and
wounded at least 1856.


The bloody disorders in the city
the worst in five months, famed
out into East and West Punjab, Sec
tions which will fall respectively
into Hindu and Pakistan domin-
ions on partition and the relin-
quishment of British rule today and
tomorrow.


Tension Blamed for Outbursts.


Tension over the expected report
of boundary commissioner fixing
the border lines between the two
dominions in the divided Punjab
was blamed for the new outhursts
Both Moslem and on-Moslem COM
munities-mainiy Sikhs and Hindus
were described as fearful of losing
coveted territory to the other.
The Joint Defense Command on
behalf of Pakistan threw additional
troops into the disturbed areas in
an effort to restore order. Two full
brigades were expected to be rein
forced during the day by third.


The Indian press published stories
today that special military force
of the joint military command
killed 81 rioters armed with mortars,
Bren and Sten guns { automatic
weapons), at Amritsar yesterday.


Amritsar, the holy city of the
Sikhs, has been one of the prin-
cipal trouble sections in the Punjab.


Stabbings Predominate.


In Lahore, a communal register
maintained by volunteer workers
at Mayo Hospital, listed most of
the casualties as Hindus and Sikhs
who had been stabbed, but also
counted members of both communi-
ties shot by law-enforcement units.


Unofficial sources have estimated
that 95 per cent of Lahore's Hindu
and Sikh population of 100000 have
fled the city and that Lahore now
is made up predominateiy of Mos
lens.


Looking over Lahore from a tall
building today, it could be seen that
the whole western horizon was lit
up by gigantic flames and smoke
hung over the whole city.


Five Sikh temples we're ablaze and
buildings along several central
streets of the capital were burn
ing, including the famous Anarkali
Bazaar. Officials said Sikh and
Hindu shops had been looted.

Austria in the past six weeks.
Under present conditions, ne told

police are powerless to stop the kid
naping, since Investigations are
limited by regulations imposed by
the occupying powers.


Terming the charges malicious
lies" the Communist Party news
paper Volksstimme said today that
British and American occupation
authorities were operating "concen-
tration camps" with the full knowl-
edge of the Austrian government.


Meanwhile, other official Austrian
sources estimated that the actual
number of kidnapings was at least
80 and possibly more.


Mr.. Helmer said most of the kid
napings had taken place in the
Russian zone of Vienna and that in
most cases the automobiles used or
the uniforms CT the men involved
were Russian.

Seven convicts escaped from the
Tennessee State Penitentiary here

three hours later, Warden John
Harwood said.


The warden said the prisoners
escaped by crawling through a DOW
erhouse steam tunnel and that five
OF the men were recaptured almost
Immediately.


The break occurred during the
showing of a motion picture, Mr..
Harwood said, explaining that the
prisoners pushed aside a heavy iron
barrier guarding the entrance to the
steam tunnel, and made their way
through it to a powerhouse out
side the prison walls.


The escape was discovered a little
later when some of the escaped
convicts were reported seen running
along a nearby railroad track, Mr..
HarWood said

LYNCHBURG, Va, Sept. State
police here say they have uncovered
a practice, repeatedly common
among automobile dealers and
garagemen throughout the State,
which is sabotaging the identifica-
ton and registration system of auto
mobiles and leaving perpetrators OF
the act liable to criminal action.


Used-car dealers and garagemen,
according to State Police Sergt. A.
c. Elmore, have been removing
engine numbers from new blocks
placed in automobiles and stamping
on the number from the old block
taken from the car. In some cases.
the officer said. the old blocks were
rebuilt and installed in other cars,
putting on the highway two auto
mobiles with identical engine num-
bers. He added that sometimes
numbers on the old blocks have been
obliterated, leaving cars in service
without engine numbers.


Police have gone to Staunton to
check cars discovered without motor
numbers in the hope that they might
be tied in with a automobile theft
ring broken up in Amherst County
six months ago. They said garage
men told them the practice is COM
mon and has been going on for some
time.


The Amherst theft ring made use
of number switches in peddling their
stolen cars. They would buy
wrecked late-model blocks, take title
to a nonresident car through the
block number, then steal an auto
mobile to match the block At their
remote headquarters in Pleasanton,
they would disassemble the motor,
remove the original motor number
and stamp in the block number for
which they had title.

by garagemen, Sergt. Elmore said


they are playing right into the car

PoRT-DE-BOUC, France, July
s0.-Port and consular officials
looked to London today to learn the
next move In the odyssey of some
1900 Jews who were turned back
from Palestine and refused to land
in France.


The refugees, intercepted by the
British of Palestine July 1s after a
voyage from Sete, France, were
brought to this tiny Mediterranean
port, 80 miles west of Marseille, yes
terday, aboard the British transports
Ocean Vigour, Empire Rival and
Runnymede Park.


British officials on hand for the
arrival of the vessels noted what
they termed collective vote" of
the Jews to remain aboard. They
said they would report the situation
to London.


French authorities already had
asserted that they would not force
any Jews to disembark, and one re-
sponsible British official here de-
clared that use of violence to clear
the ships was unthinkable.


Sick Taken Ashore.


Ali the passengers except six per-
sons in poor health steadfastly re-
manned on the three transports in
sitdown strike against landing.
These Ska Rumanian Jew, his
wife and four other women-went
ashore last night. One woman, re-
covering from pneumonia, was
borne on a stretcher.


All three ships were reported des-
perately low on food supplies. The
British apparently had not prepared
for an extended stay in French
waters nor for further voyage with
the refugees.


French charities prepared to send
stocks of canned milk, bread, noodles
and other foods to the Runnymede
Park early today, since her provi-
sions were said to be near exhaus-
ton. They were expected to supply
the other two ships before noon.


French authorities polled the
ships passengers soon after the
vessels dropped anchor here and
reported that large number had

Is Americans on Ships.

been truly representative. But when

the results final, the British did not
press the point.

the crew of the Exodus of 1947'' had
been put among the refugees by
mistake. They stayed aboard the
ships.

transports late yesterday urging the
refugees not to land. The British
said the launch had been sent out

ish group committed to assistance
of unauthorized immigration into

Gated they planned local protest.
Later French police arrested those
in the launch. verified their ident-
ity papers and then freed them. !

YUMA, Colo. Aug. II (P.-Four
persons were dug from the shat

yesterday after % cars snapped

building, scattering pieces more

way and ended up in a jumbled

and splintered wood and were cut
out.

later over a sidetrack while section
workers began clearing the wreck
age and rebuilding nearly quarter
mile of track. -.--

cabinet holding its second "crisis
meeting in eight days. yesterday
drafted new austerity program
which is expected to be announced
later this week by Prime Minister
Attlee.


Mr.. Attlee and other ministers
interrupted their vacations for the
four-hour meeting, which reliable
informants said was called to dis
cuss emergency plans for curtailed
food rations, increased hours for
miners and reactions to Britain's
sudden sterling freeze" last week,


Silent cabinet ministers waved to
crowds of curious spectators as they
left No. 10 Downing street, but
brushed aside questions about the
meeting that brought top Labor
Party leaders together. There was
speculation that Parliament might
be called into special session.


The British Press Association re-
ported that new austerity plan"
woula be announced from the prime
minister's Office later this week.
This was an apparent move to lay
the crisis program before next
weeks annual convention of the
Trades Union Congress, a powerful
force in the ruling Labor Party.


Presence of Food Minister John
Strachey at the cabinet meeting
-was~seen as. an indication that the
new food rationing program would
be made Known shortly. Mr.. Stra-
chey does not hold formal cabinet
rank, and does not attend policy
making cabinet sessions unless food
supplies are under discussion.

field"

which it is now finding out 1t can

Nauru, last of the former League
inundated Pacific islands to be pro-
posed for United Nations trustee
ship, has made many of its natives
wealthy. Superrich fertilizer isl
the pay dirt on this 8-square-mile
oval just south of the Equator, says
the National Geographic Society.
| Under German ownership prior to
World War I, Nauru's phosphate
diggings were worked by an Anglo
German company which installed
machinery and dock facilities for
exporting the fertilizer in big vol
ume. Later, commission under
the British mandate took charge OF
production.


Phosphate from Nauru became
responsible for increased fertility
of millions of farm acres in Aus
tralia, which took more than half
the small islands output. Nauru's
prdouct doubled the Australian
wheat crop.


So important had this fertilizer
become to Australian agriculture
that during World War II, with
Japan holding Nauru, phosphates
were shipped to Australia from half
yay around the world-from dis
tsnt Florida and from the, Red Sea
area. Nauru, west of the Gilbert
Islands, is Its miles northeast OF
Australia.


The exploitation of Naurus mill
lions of tons of age-old guano de-
posits dates only from 1900. The
open quarries we're worked by a
thousand imported Chinese laborers,
but phosphate revolutionized the life
of native Nauruans, about 1000 in
all.


Prior to 1900 the fortunate Maui
ruans were those who held the
islands coastal strip with its border
of profitable coconut palms. Copra
WAS Nauru's cash crop. The poorer
natives possessed only worthless
inland plateau land, rising as much
as 1877 feet above the sea.


Phosphate reversed the material
{prosperity. The inland holders be-
gan to receive royalties from their
rich acres which enabled them to
supply their wants without labor.


Nauru had been known to Amer
ican whalers for decades prior to
1888, the year Germany annexed
the island. Because of its phos-
phate, it has often been called the
richest island in the South Seas.

For more than half century the byline
of Samuel G. Blythe was familiar symbol
OF American news writing at its best.
His chosen field was that of politics, and
none of his contemporaries was more
intimately acquainted with its ramiflca-
tions, its characters, its effects. Between
1886, when he joined the staff Of the
Rochester Democrat and Chronicle, and
1910, when at last he retired, he knew
every President and practically every other
important figure on the Government side
of the American scene His reporting was
factual, his interpretations scrupulously
objective. Yet his work did not lack
warmth and sympathy. He wrote with a
frankly vital concern for people as human
beings Mere statistics meant little to
him. What he wanted to discover-and

brought the Exodus 1947 Jews to
Germany.


Some kicking, screaming Jews,
their heads bloodied in 90 minutes

bodily from the transport, the Run
nymede Park, after a Shutdown strike
against landing.


An official British casualty re-
port said SO Jews, including Is wom-
en-, were injured and that 10 of

were hospitalized with injuries.


Correspondents on the dockside

The violence attending the I'M

The steel-helmeted troops under

The six young Scandinavian Scien-
lists who comprised the crew of the
Kon-Tiki raft expedition reported
by radio yesterday that they are
trying to salvage the remains of
their 45-foot balsa-wood raft, after
unwittingly carrying historical ac-
curacy to the ultimate by crashing
against a reef in the Tuamotu
Archipelago -easternmost chain of
the Polynesian Islands-just as they
had surmised before their departure
that the first Peruvian settlers of
the area were carried ashore by
the prevailing winds and currents.


Thor Heyerdahl, 32-year-old Nor
wegian ethnologist who led the ex-
pedition, also reported today that
''the strength and shape of our
raft and the courage and discipline
of our crew permitted every one
to reach safety unhurt.


The men first got ashore August
Z, and some since then improvised
a small radio set with which they
contact the outside world.


Burden of radio commuhica-


ton with the men Is being borne


by two young amateur radio


operators in Los Angeles, Har-


old Kempel and Frank Cuevas,


both members of the American


Radio Relay League. The bulk of


earlier reports from the Kon-


Tiki crew, both to North Amer


ican Newspaper Alliance and


through other amateurs-to the


mems families in Norway and


Sweden, has gone through these


men)


The men hope to find natives to
help them in their salvage opera
tions, but the innumerable islands
of the Tuamotu Archipelago are
sparsely settled. Small groups of
natives live along the shores of
occasional lagoons, from which they
extract the pearls and pearl shell
as a livelihood.


The islands of the. group are
mostly coral atolls, much like Kwa-
jalein, Peleliu, Tarawa and others
on which American troops fought
during the war. The Tuamotus have
a somewhat cooler climate, how
ever, and greater variety Of vege-
tation.


Had the men attempted to land
at Raroia six weeks later they would
have met the strong southwest swell
which heralds the hurricane season
and makes all landings, even those
on sandy beaches, most perilous
undertakings.

good health and spirits, and they
have now. decorated their camp, sit
uat ted under several tall palm trees,
| with Norwegian flag and one from

zvai Leuni, Jewish underground

young Tel Aviv municipal clerk
whom it credited with plotting and
leading the Acre Prison delivery
on May 5.


Cohen, the citation" said. was
fatally wounded in the delivery,
which freed several hundred pris-
oners-of whom 20 Jews and 118
Arabs are reported still at large.


Irgun said that Cohen. who was
26 on the day of the raid, had
served five years in the British
army, during which he got a mill
tary medal and was mentioned twice
in dispatches" 1t added that Cohen
had published literary works in
Hebrew monthly magazines.


Nobody had any suspicion" Irgun
declared, that this young and gifted
ex-soldier and clerk of the Tel Aviv
municipality was a commander of
Irgun and that he succumbed while
carrying out plan he worked out
to free his comrades from Acre
prison."


The Citation" said that Cohen,
wearing an army captains uniform,
had led a raiding party over the roof
of a Turkish bath adjoining the
prison and had blasted window to
gain entrance.


He was shot, along with four pris-
oners and two other raiders, while
trying to make his getaway, Irgun
said,

SEATTLE. April S.-Nine persons
lost their lives last night when a
heavy North Coast Lines bus col
lided with an oil truck and then
plunged into the Duwamish River
running alongside the Pacific high
way near here.


Twelve other passengers and the
bus driver, Melvin D. Long, %, OF
Olympia, Wash, survived, some with
severe but none with critical in
juries.


Early today seven Of the dead had
been identified, Coroner John P.
Brill, jr., said. They were:


Telford F. Smithee, Seattle, the
truck driver.


Darlene Wick, 8, Portland, Greg.


Erwin Burian, Tacoma, Wash.


Mrs. Helga Wick, Seattle, grand
mother of Darlene.


James Mark Sullivan. Seattle.


Lydia M. Gresham, Seattle.


mIS. 6Wlu ouI ldtl. 1dtSiilds


Rescuers Wade Into River.


Two women have not been iden-
tilted.


Heroic rescue work by eyewitnesses
and motorists, who waded into the
river and climbed atop the two
thirds submerged bus, prevented a
heavier death toll


The first rescuers at the scene
hacked holes into the roof to pull
to safety passengers who were fight
ing for air inside.


The heroism of little Darlene Wick
was credited by survivors with saving
many lives.


They said that amid the panic
inside the partially submerged bus,
the 6-year-old child stood calmly
and In an even voice called direc-
tions to volunteer rescuers cutting
through the top.


She stood there in the aisle, they
said, with the water rising around
her. The help she summoned for
her fellow passengers arrived too
late to save her life. She was
trapped in the wreckage as she at
tempted to free herself and drowned.
The bus driver escaped by kicking
out the windshield, while number
of men got out without assistance
and clung to driftwood in the river
until rescued.


Work In Rain.


Deputy sheriffs, police and State
patrolmen worked in heavy rain
with artificial respiration and pull
motors.


The bus continued on short way
after the collision, then veered to
the left, snapped off a telephone
pole, i1urtled a 15-foot-high bank
and plunged into the river, finally
ending up against pilings 25 feet out,
The front of the bus was crushed
In for about feet. The heavy
vehicle f1oated a minute or two in
the water while those inside fought
10 escape.


An emergency door on one side
popped open and William E. Cum
mings, Spokane youth, worked his
way out.


Soon auto spotlights were flashed
on the wreckage and the rescue
work started. Screams of those in
side could be heard as the rescuers
cut at the roof to reach them.


More than an hour went by be-
fore the bus was brought to the
surface and 1t was determined all
passengers had been removed.

in atom bombed Nagasaki have
shown increases of from so to 300
per cent over the normal yield, Taxed
Furuno, Nagasaki prefectural agri-

LONDON, Sept. 24-The British
government, fearing a very nasty
situation" might develop from anti
Semitism, has ordered police
campaign against orators who de-
nounce Jews, a government source
said today

the present government policy street
speakers who support Fascist ideol-
ogies but do not denounce Jews
would not be molested.

Secretary Chuter EIDE had instructed
police to take fairly full notes" of
anti-Semitic street-corner speeches

land Yards legal division. He added
that the government would prose-
cute such speakers on charges of
melting to violence, whenever a case
can be made out.


The informant said the objective
of the ORDER was "the protection of
the Jewish community and the pre-
vention of disorder"

The Ramadier cabinets fight against
imitation goes on However, the strain is
terrific. Inf1ationary pressure is not con-
fined to labor, though labor troubles get
most of the headlines. And even on the
labor front, current government successes
may prove to be illusory.


Premier Ramadier faced major chal-
lenge when the gas and electric workers
threatened to strike if their wage demands
were not granted. Since those vital in
dustries are now nationalized, this would
have meant a strike against the govern
ment. Accordingly, the Premier invoked
a wartime statute not yet repealed under
which the gas and electric workers could
be 'requisitioned" for national service,
the equivalent of mobilization into the
army, with drastic penalties for dis
obedience. The first reaction of the
workers was one of defiance, and there
was even some talk of a general strike.


However, it soon became evident that
neither side wanted to precipitate a show
down which might have incalculakle
political consequences. So compromise
has been reached under which the workers
will have their claims for higher wages
re-eXamined and meanwhile will be
granted production bonuses" that can
senSibly increase their take-home pay.
And it seems evident that this is pattern
which the government is ready to apply
to other labor disputes.


The question now is whether such
bonuses, if generally granted, will be
camouf1aged wage increases that will dis
rupt the present precarious equilibrium
between wages and prices, thereby starting
the infiationary spiral which Ramadier
seeks desperately to avoid. The govern
ment holds that since the bonuses will be
paid only for increased production, the
net result will not be inflationary. But
other economic groups hold the contrary
and redouble their demands. Businessmen
large and small, shopkeepers, white-collar
workers, I war veterans, and others, all
insist on equivalent relief from the wage
price squeeze which now grips them, in
one way or another. There is even wide
spread campaign for the abolition of all
governmental controls and a return to the
law of supply and demand The govern
ment denounces such proposal as mad

GALVESTON, Tex, April H.
Three Of the six surviving crew
members of the French freighter
Grandcamp in a hospital here last
night told how they fought to sub
due the blaze before the ship ex-
ploded, setting off the chain of
explosions which wrecked Texas
City.


Contrary to reports that guam
/ tity Of black powder on the Grand
camp caused the explosion which
spread through the thriving indus
trial section, Morris lie Brozec, So
lyear-old seaman who worked in the
engine room, said the fire originated
In hold No. 4.


The hold was partly filled with
the fertilizer Tuesday and the hatch
was closed for the night, LIE Brozec,
the only English-speaking member
of the group, said.


Wednesday morning when the
| stevedoring crew reported for work


the hold was opened by Julien
Gueril, the ships carpenter, who is
occupying one of the cots in the
crews ward at st. Mary's Infirm-
Iary here.
IT saw a little smoke rising from


the fertilizer when I opened the


hatch," Gueril said. "I picked up
a fire extinguisher and started


spraying the cargo.


When the smoke started coming
out bigger I closed the hatch and


turned on steam In the compart-
tment. The fire kept burning Until
| 1t made enough pressufs to blow of
the cover"


Pieces Of the ship, weighing hum
dreds of pounds, were blown 1000
feet in the air and some large blocks
of metal landed in the business dis
trict a mile from the ship.
The crew members saia- the fire
evidently started when the hatch
was first opened at 8 am.
lie Brozec said the ships captain
was on the dock making a telephone
call when the fire started. The
first mate, man named Mazarguil,
ordered the ship abandoned about
$3.50. The crew. except the surviv-
ing members, joined the stevedoring
crew on the dock.


Three of the survivors went to a
nearby refreshment stand, while
three others started walking through
the plant to the home Of a friend.
The explosion collapsed the stand
on the crewmen and the operator.


The sailors struggled loose after the
blast, but the operator was dead.


"The explosion was many times


worse than W. bomb" said Guy


Saucey, who fought with the Free


French during World War II.


"Our ears were bleeding and we


were covered with oil and dirt" he


added. I'VE walked around in a


daze until some one took US to the


hospital"
Each of the six survivors suffered


similar injuries. They are being OBJ


served for possible fractured skulls,
their hands and feet are swollen and


they suffered severe cuts on their
| bodies.


The crewnen said the ships cargo


consisted of sisa1 from Havana, cot
ton and peanuts from Houston and
the fertilizer from Texas City. The

engagement between the battleship
New Mexico and Newark's squirt

naught arrived outside the harbor

mornings tide.

New Mexico stood five miles south

determined to prevent the decom-

NEW YORK, Aug. 30.-Prices were
firm in the cotton textile market
during the past week with demand
still centering on print cloths.


AS, offerings were scarce, business
was limited to scattered lots for
spot and future delivery. Some SELL
ing houses Indicated they would not
release substantial amounts of goods
until after the September 8 Gov
ernment cotton crop report which
will give a better idea of supply
prospects.


Merchants generally expressed the
belief that buying of goods would
continue to hold at a high rate for
some months since several mills
already are making fair sales of
print cloths and broadcloths for the
second quarter of next year. The
outlook for heavy industrial goods is
considered less favorable.


Demand for drills and pocketing
twills improved after a long period
of inactivity and light weight sheet
ings were sought.


Interest in worsted goods for mems
wear continued to exceed supplies
and more mills were expected to
announce spring lines and prices
after the Labor Day holiday.


With several of the leading mills
deferring fourth quarter allotments
until next month, rayon goods were
scarce.

Wherever people have gathered
this fall and winter, the talk sooner
or later has swung around to the
new look" Now comes something
new and different in the art Of carv-
ing the Christmas turkey. The ac-
companying pictures show the cary
ing being accomplished with the
turkey on It's side, instead of being
done in the traditional style. Carv-
ing experts have different opinions,
but many people think the new side
method of carving makes the pro-
cess much easier.


Step /: Remove the Wing Portion.
Grasp the wing tip firmly between
thumb and fingers, lift UP, and sever
between the first and second joints.
Drop the wing tip and first-joint
portion to the side platter. The
second joint is left attached to the
bird.


Step 2: Remove the Drumstick.
Grasp the end Of the drumstick and
lift 1t up and away from the body,
disjointing 1t at the thigh; then
transfer the drumstick to the side
platter for slicing the meat. The
thigh Is left attached to the bird.


Step 8: Slice the Drumstick Meat.
Hold the drumstick upright at
convenient angle and cut down, par
alleI with the bone, turning the leg
to make uniform slices.


Step 4: Slice the Thigh Meat.
Anchoring the fork where it is most
convenient to steady the bird, cut
slices parallel to the body until the
bone is reached, and remove the

text:
To the Editor of The Star:


There is tradition of one of our Indian
nations-I have forgotten which-that runs as
follows:


The Divine Father had a number OF sons.
All these brothers had different colored skins:
one white, one red one yellow, one brown, one
black. Their Father put them in different
parts of the world, giving them each separate
country to live in. He hoped by this means to
satisfy them and their progeny and that there
would be peace. But the white son was different
in every way from his brothers and his progeny
unfortunately inherited his quarrelsome and
greedy disposition. Though they proved clever
in getting what they wanted and in devising
means of killing each other and saving them
selves from work, they developed very poor
memories. They did not keep their promises.
They would not distinguish between right and
wrong.


So the Divine Father taught them how to
write, in order that they could put their
thoughts on paper and they would not escape
them. Then he showed them how to print and
their promises were put into treaties, by which
they vowed to end wars. But this did no good.


They quarreled about what their treaties and
their printed books meant, they quarreled about
religion, they quarreled about trade They
could not agree about anything. They had
many wars among themselves Not satisfied
with the way their Father had made the part
Of the earth he had given them, they proceeded
to tear 1t up and make it over again. After
which, being dscontented with their own
country, they, went forth to take the countries
which were their brothers birthright.


After this had gone on for some time, the
Divine Father sent them across the Big Sea
Water to see the fresh. unspoiled condition of
the country where the red people lived The
first white people who came over had been SO
busy cheating each other that they could not
live in simple, natural manner and the red,
people had to teach them to raise corn or they
would have starved. They repaid this kindness
by killing their benefactors and taking their
land. They seemed always intent upon destruc-
tion. When the red people were out of their
way, they still continued destroying themselves.
Even now, because they are constantly wasting
the earth's precious stores, they are always in
need.


The Divine Father has made many dispensa-
tions for the past sins of h.. hayward white
children. When will His patience be exhausted?


TEKARIHOKEN.

The House today approved leg
islation to permit laid-off Gov
ernment employees to withdraw
their contributions to the civil
service retirement system.


Under terms of the bill, dismissed
Government employees with less than
10 years service to their credit can
withdraw their retirement money.
The present law permits only those
workers with less than five years of
Federal service to draw out their
money.


Sponsored by Representative
Jones, Republican, of Washington
the measure now goes to the Senate.


Thousands of Federal employees
now losing their jobs during the
reduction in force program would
benefit under the bill. These en-
ployes entered the Government in
1910 and 1941 and, consequently, are
not eligible under the present law
to withdraw their money.


The Jones bill, however, allows
them to withdraw their contribu-
tions, averaging about $500 or $400
per person. Government employees
are not entitled to unemployment
compensation benefits, and refunded
retirement money would help tide
over dismissed workers until they
find new jobs.


The provision in the Jones bill is
also contained in the Langer-Cha-
vez-Stevenson Omnibus civi, serv-
ice retirement bill, but sponsors
of the Jones measure decided to
press for it's enactment after it was
decided that the chances for the
omnibus legislation were none too
good.


Under the present law, once an
employe has completed five years of
Federal service he must leave his
contributions in the civil service re-
tirement fund until he reaches the
age of 81, when annlities begin.

The danger to gardeners from the
wood tick, carrier of Rocky Mountain
spotted fever, may be lessened con-
siderably by the use Of DDT. accord
ing to the Agriculture Department
Bureau Of Entomology and Plant
Quarantine.


Ticks are making their appearance
now and will continue active until
early fall. A number of deaths have
been reported each year.


For control in small garden areas,
the bureau recommends busting a
10 per cent DDT powder over grass,
weeds and shrubs at the rate of
from 2 to pounds to the acre. For
back yards, vacant lots and child
recreation areas l ounce to 1000
square feet is recommended.


Bureau studies made last year
indicate the ticks usually move from
overgrown areas to paths or roads,
probably Attracted by the scent of
dogs and other animals. Hence,
paths throughout the grounds, and
roads along the property should be
busted. This will kill the ticks where
they have concentrated and also will
kill ticks coming into this area for
some time after the treatment.


In addition to the busting, the
bureau said, daily body inspections
for ticks should be regular house.
hold routine. A tick does not usually
transmit the disease until after it
has been attached for more than
five hours. The ticks should be re-
moved from the body with tweezers,
never with the fingers. the bureau
warned.

PATUXENT, Md, Sept. 90
Landing tests are under way here
on the Navy's newly developed
lighted highway" on Chesapeake
Bay which may make night land
ings for seaplanes as safe as day
time landings.


Called a seadrome, this "high-
way has been developed at the
Naval Air Test Center in an effort
to give pilots contact perspective
as the seaplane settles down toward
the water.


Simple buoy lights for seaplane
lanes on harbors, rivers and lakes
have been used for number of
years. But they have not been ade-
quate and both military and civilian
pilots have lost their lives because
they could not determine their exact
altitude.


For the first time lights beneath
the surface of the water are being
used.


Bulb Filaments Crack.


Different types of buoys and diff
ferent type lights are being tried
out in the seadrome which extends
from the air base out into the bay.


First problem encountered was
the cracking, after short use, of the
fllaments in the light bulbs. At
first it was thought the tempera-
ture differential between the bulb
and the cold water was responsible.


Finally, engineers discovered
through delicate measuring instru-
ments that it was vibration-car-
ried through the water from ships
propellers, wind and other causes
which caused the short life of the
filaments.


Stronger filaments, both for the
IS and watt bulbs being used in
the experiment, so far are holding
up against vibration.


Barnacles a Problem.


Barnacles also present problem.
Engineers are trying to lick this
obstacle by coating the glass lenses
with different oils and types of
grease.


It also was discovered that the
copper screen, first used to protect
the lenses, gathered mud, and other
metal screens are being tried to
keep clouding by mud and silt at
minimum.


This project is considered signifi-
cant because interest in seaplanes
Is increasing among private flyers
and many new seaplane bases are
being built.

Many women are uncomfortable
because Of backache. especially dur
ing pregnancy and often afterwards.
Whenever a woman has a persistant
backache she should consult her
physician. However, this Is often
caused by poor posture and Is ex-
aggerated during pregnancy.


At no time is good carriage more
Important! The unusual weight in
front which the muscles must bear
tend to tilt the pelvis forward.
Sometimes even after the baby
arrives, the forward tilt will con-
tinue thus causing backache. This,
plus the danger of a fall, make
low heels the only sensible foot
wear for the pregnant woman. High
heels exaggerate the forward tilt
and throw the body off balance.


Even when pregnancy Is not pres
ent, a heavy pendulous abdomen
may have the same effect. Your
physician should advise you con-
cerning exercise during pregnancy
and will tell you how soon you can
begin exercising after the delivery
of your child. There are many mo-
tions which are helpful in recon-
ditioning abdominal muscles and
improving carriage.


The following exercise is correc-
tive to sway-back and constipation:
Lie on your back with your legs
straight and your arms resting on
the floor at your sides. Bend your
left knee up close to your stomach.
Grasp the knee with your hands and
pull hard. Return left leg and arm
to the floor. The next time, bend
your right knee close to your tummy.
grasp with both hands and pull.
Return right leg and arms to floor.
Continue, alternating left and right.

With them went. also, part of the

financial support.


American moVieStarS captivated

With the approval by the House Appro-
priations Committee of proposed allot-
ment of $1,700000 for purchase of site
and preparation of plans, Washington's
new hospital center has been brought a
step closer to realization. Congress cannot
move too quickly to bring this vital
project into being, for delay in the under
taking means further prolongation of local
hospital conditions properly described as
disgraceful (See Building More Hospi-
tails" elsewhere on this page.)


The reduced sum allowed for acquisition
of land for the center is justified by the
fact that the new institution will be built
on part of the Naval Observatory tract,
already owned by the Government, and on
the adjoining District-owned site OF the
Industrial Home School, A much larger
appropriation would have been required
If private land had been involved. This
saving should not be lost to Washington's
badly deteriorating hospitals, however. 1t
could well be added to larger sum which
Congress has been asked to appropriate
for noncenter hospitals.


Under present plans, only Emergency,
Garfield and Episcopal Hospitals will
benefit from the center project. The orig
inal bill for the center contained a pro-
vision to aid other local hospitals, but the
noncenter institutions were excluded when
the authorization finally was enacted.
However, Representative Mary Norton of
New Jersey has introduced bill to provide
Federal grants for the other deserving
hospitals This bill is pending before the
House District Committee.


The three institutions which are in
cluded in the proposed center are not the
only ones here that need assistance. The
center will provide substantial relief for
Washingtons hospital needs, but even
after its 1900 beds are ready to serve the
sick there will still be a shortage of 1850
beds here Passage of the Norton bill
would pave the way for reconstruction and
additions, outside the center, that would
60 long way toward eliminating condi-
tions which have shocked committees Of
lay and professional Investigators. These
shameful conditions should not be toll
Grated in any enlightened community.

stand on the occupation record to
date. Some commonwealth spokes-
men, however, have voiced a desire
for further, more thorough social
and political reform, and harsher
economic terms in the peace treaty.
Naturally, the Japanese side with
Gen. Macarthur.


Critics Debated.


Gen. MacArthur's aggressive &C
ton in making this primarily an
American occupation. under Presi-
dent Truman's policy of 1915, was
approved by all II interested ma
tions in a recent Far Eastern Com
mission policy statement. And this,
in effect, Debated international
critics who have condemned the
generals high handedness," among
other things.


The Supreme Commander was
the first to voice the request for an
early peace treaty, and to urge that
work begin this fall, even If the
German treaty remained unsigned.
Other nations fell into line, and the

nouncement came through on
schedule.

munist forces in North China cut

nouncement that American mill

drawal by damaging the railway

rines, and was different from the

teens with bands of Communist

were convinced, however, that the
withdrawal of all American media
tors would invite heavier fighting
They predicted that both. the gov.
ernment and the Communists woule
try to make drives in Manchuria
and North China.


While both government and Com.
munist leaders speculated over thu
effects Of the departure of tht
Americans, informed sources ir
Nanking predicted that all Com.

territory would be closed with thu
possible exception of Markings.
They pointed out that government
military commanders long had com.
planned of the presence of top
notch Communists in Marking
Shanghai and Chungking, where
they were able to observe and re-
port to Yenan.


Under terms Of last years agree
ment establishing mediation ma
chinery, Secretary of State Mar
shall, then special American envoy
pledged that the United States
would return Communists from
executive headquarters at Peiping
as we'll as liaison officers, to Com.
munist territory.


Withdrawal of the United State.
Marines, which American source!
in Peiping said would follow thu
departure of the LOCO Army ane
civilian personnel from Peipins
quarters, will leave few American
military forces in China.


There still will remain the Navy:
training school in Tsingtao and the
military advisory group in China
both small. Either could pull out
easily on orders from Washington


Despite the danger that both sides
may come out shooting with ali
guns, the American withdrawal was
expected here to meet not only the
wishes of Yenan but a fairly large
section of public opinion in gov
ernnent China.

said she was getting ready for bed.

NEW YORK, Aug. 5.-Rodney
Smith, 81, known throughout
the world as Gipsy Smith, British
evangelist, died of heart all
ment aboard the liner Queen
Mary yesterday.


The death of the man who was
born in gypsy tent and made the
world his field for active evangelism
was announced when the giant ship
reached port today on her first post
war commercial voyage.


Mr.. Smith had visited the United
States more than 80 times, circled
the globe twice, worked in South
Africa and spent three and one-half
years in France during World War
I. When American troops were leav-
ing for home after the Armistice,
Gipsy Smith was in Paris to preach
farewell to them.


For his work in France his coun-
try awarded him the Order of the
British Empire.


A few hours before his death he
had insisted on being carried to
the top deck of the liner to greet
some friends.


Mrs. Smith, who accompanied the
noted evangelist. said her husband
mad made the trip for his health.

MOSCOW, July 25.-The interna-
tional fur auction in Leningrad is
going full swing with more than 100
foreign buyers present, including, a
large group from the United States,
in the first large scale invasion of
foreign businessmen into the Soviet
Union since before the war.


According to reports from Lenin-
grad the auction, being held under
the auspices of Soyuzpushnina
Soviet fur marketing organization
is marked by heavy buying, solid
prices and good furs.


Philip Dickman, representing
Lands Bros. and United American
Furs, said on the telephone from
Leningrad that sables, ermine, and
Persian lamb represented the pick
of the large lot being offered.


Mr. Dickman said the choice items
largely are being picked off by
American representatives of many
fur brokers and individual firms.
The auction formally opened July
81 with a. large banquet given by
Soyuzpushnina for attending buyers.
Actually, however, the buyers ar
rived July 10 in order to inspect the
lots which were on exhibition.


Since July 81 sales have been going
on every day from 10 am. to 8 pm.
This intensive schedule has tired
buyers and seriously interfered with
the gala social life under Leningrad's s
white nights which had been char
acteristic of the sales before the war


The buyers are housed in the we'll
known, comfortable Astoria Hotel.
Sales proceed in the famous Fur
Auctions Building devoted solely to
Russia's large fur trade and designed
particularly to handle auctions.


The sales will end July rs when
visiting buyers will leave and Mos
cows colony of American fur buyers
regularly living in Thea Metropole
Hotel in the Soviet capital will re-
turn to sit out the winter and carry
on their regular, little advertised
business of handling Russia's major
export to the United States.

NEW YORK. Aug. 22.-Retail
trade, aided by cooler weather in
some areas, remained this week at
the level of the previous week and
was slightly above the 1916 period.
Dun & Bradstreet reported today.


Promotions of fall merchandise
increased In the week ended We'd
nesday, and clearance sales were
fewer.


| Consumers, still discriminating as
to Quality and price, found sub
stantial qualities of most foods
readily available, remained inter-
ested in mems clothing while pay.
ing scant attention to furs, mill
linery and jewelry and bought
heavily of household supplies and
bedding.


Demand for fresh fruits and
vegetables was good and house
wives in some sections purchased
large stocks for home canning.
Consumption Of dairy products, soft
drinks and beer increased and the
known brands of canned goods were
popular.


While markdowns continued on
summer clothing and some types Of
shoes, the number of apparel clear
ance sales decreased. Back-to-
school items were popular.


Nationally advertised major ap-
pliances and high quality dining
and bedroom furniture were scarce.
Increased vacation travel led to a
demand for tires and automobile
supplies.


Retail volume was estimated by
Dun & Bradstreet at from per
cent below to per cent above a
year ago. Declines occurred in New
England the Middle West and
South. Increases were largest on
the Pacific Coast and in the South
west. The Northwest and East also
showed improvement.


Wholesale volume in the week rose
slightly above the preceding week
and was moderately higher than
last year Buying continued to be
cautious and increased costs and
slow deliveries in some lines trou-
bled retailers.
headline:
Retail Trade Stays
Slightly Over 1916

Jews injured, one critically, and

tion which came after military pa
trolls, with the aid of a curfew, had
enforced an uneasy truce through
the night.


The unofficial figures indicated
this casualt ytoll since Sunday:
Dead, eight Jews and five Arabs:
wounded, 43 Jews and IS Arabs.


Along the squalid market places
where the Jewish community abuts
on the Arab. belligerent youths ap-
peared on the alert for new prova-
cations. More than half the small.
dingy shops were closed and there
was little traffic.


Police had hoped--apparently in
vain-that the morning had brought
the end of the four days of strife.
Last nights curfew kept some 30
600 Jews and Arabs in their homes.


1t was the first time Arab territory
had been under curfew since the
Arab rising Of l936-l939.

AS II tney old not have enough
worries with things as they are, the
Nations safety experts are begin
ming to worry about potential perils
of the dawning age of atomic energy,
jet propulsion and similar scientific
marvels. More than seven thousand
specialists on accident prevention
attending the annual Safety Con-
vention and Exposition in New York
City have been warned to prepare
for dire new accident hazards in the
era of unleashed atomic power and
supersonic speeds that lies ahead.


1t Is certainly not too early for
the safety experts to start thinking
about the accident problems of the
future, even though they have their
hands full in these relatively slow
moving times. The harnessing of
the atom for industrial use will mean
new kinds of danger for those en-
ployed on the project-risks, like
radiation exposure, requiring new
educational campaigns and new
safeguards for workers and the pub
lie. And, just as highway and air.
way authorities are exerting their
best efforts to promote safety of
travel, along come jet motors and
rockets to push speeds higher than
ever and, withal, to bring new
dangers to human life and limb.


These dangers will not, of course,
deter man from venturing further
and further in the field of scientific
progress. On the contrary, the very
dangers involved constitute a chal-
lenge which serves only to spur the
inventors and engineers to greater
accomplishments. These bold and
determined pioneers are running
risks far graver than those which
will confront the later users of
atomic power or the passengers of
rocket aircraft. AS with the rail-
road, the automobile and the air
plane, the accident hazards will
decrease as mans experience with
and knowledge of the new devices
increase-and as safety experts con-
tinue their worthwhile campaign
to reduce the accident toll on the
ground and in the air. Truly the
safety experts job is never done.

Whooping cranes are nearing
extinction. Many feel that in short
time the last whooping crane will
disappear. Only intelligent cooper

this from occurring.


The goal is to find ways and
means to restore whooping cranes
to their former haunts. The whoop-
ing crane, one of Our most colorful
and largest birds, is fast vanishing
from the sight of ALL


Airplanes have been used effec-
lively in locating them. Over the
Arkansas National Wildlife Refuge
near Austwell, Tex, Is whooping
cranes were seen in the winter Of
1945.


The whooping cranes range now
extends from Northern Canada to
Texas and Louisiana and possibly
into Mexico. Winters are spent in
the South and summers in the
North. The birds would have to be
studied during their nesting sea-
son. Only two birds have been seen
in recent years near Vermilion Bay
in Louisiana where a few years ago
there were Is.


In the Middle Western States and
in Canada great numbers nested,
the place livened with their whoops
and beauty.


Today, cranes are among the
wariest of birds in the world. Every
bird expects death from man. Years
have proven that the pure white
plumaged body has been an ire
sistible target for the gunner,


Whooping cranes stand four feet
high with a seven-foot wingspread.
The plumage, with the exception Of
black wing tips and featherless head
and cheeks of bright red, is pure
white. The long bill is dark green
ish-vellow, the legs and feet dull
black. Not to forget that If the
cranes windpipe were uncoiled It
would measure five feet-which en-
ables it to give the long, loud,
mighty whoops.


In fight the bird in spite of size
is very graceful. Rising from the
ground with effortless motion, TAX
ing off with little climbing steps of
the airway, legs stretched out
straight lined with the body--a
beautiful white ship in the air.

Crossing this threshold was
the beginning of the road
back for Sally and her family.


She and Eddie were married
at the age of 16. Eddie's
mother always resented the
marriage. When a second
baby came and Eddie lost his
job, it wasn't hard for his
mother to persuade him to
come back home.


Sally kept the children at
her parents home. But in
the midst of one of her
fathers drunken TRADES, she
had to take the children and
leave. She wandered to the
park fronting the General
Accounting Office. Covering
the babies with her coat, she
sat on a bench and pondered.
Finally, she slept.


When she awoke, the sun
was shining on an emblem
she recognized across the
street. She gathered up the
children, and mounted the
steps beside the red shield of
the Salvation Army emer-'
gency home.


There were baths, break
fast, a long rest, for all three.
And later a social worker to
whom Sally could pour out
her troubles. Sally still loved
Eddie. The social worker con-
tacted him; reminded him of
his responsibility to his fam
lily. Finally, Eddie came back.


Four years passed, but Eddie
had begun to drink heavily.
He walked out again. A sec
ond time, the Salvation Army
worker brought the husband
and wife together. There was
another reconciliation. 1t was
while he was overseas during
the war that Eddie really
began to realize how hard he
had made things.


Today, Sally and Eddie and
their children are a happy
family. They are members of
the Salvation Army Corps.
Their children are in the
corps youth organizations. A
new baby will be christened
soon.


The Community Chest,
through your contributions,
made it possible for Sally to
find a haven under the red
shield, and start the road back
to happiness. The Community
Chest is your once-a-year
chance. Star Staff Photo.

BOSTON, Nov. 19.-The pell nell
rush of both Boston teams into
baseball trade marts, with apparent
good results, has revived hopes for
an "up and down Commonwealth
avenue" all-Boston World Series in
1948.


The Red Sox, dethroned as Amer
ican League titlists last season when
they finished shade behind second
place Detroit, have gained two start
ing pitchers and a top flight infielder
from the st. Louis Browns.


The Braves have obtained an out
fielder with a stronger arm than
any of their gardeners had last year,
a lefthanded- hitting catcher and
two pitchers who seem qualified to
bolster the not-so-strong relief corps
of 1947 when the Tribe finished only
eight games of the National League
pace.


Pennant Flame Rekindled.


Acquisition of such performers by
the Red Sox as Pitchers Jack Kramer
and Ellis Kinder and Shortstop Ver-
non (Junior) Stephens really has
rekindled the pennant flame among
the many supporters Of the club
which now has the winning Joe NC
Carthy as field pilot and the canny
Joe Cronin as general manager.


In obtaining Jimmy Russell from
the Pittsburgh Pirates the Braves
now have an outfielder who pos
sesses something resembling a good
arm. Last season none OF the outer
gardeners in tribal regalia could
drill the ball in from the open
spaces with consistent speed and
accuracy.


In AL Lyons, also obtained from
the Pirates, the Tribe has a pitcher
who can throw hard for a few in
nings, filling another 1947 void. The
Braves also plan to use Jim Pender-
CAST, big, strong left handler OBJ
tained from Syracuse, as relief
pitcher next season.


Bill Salkeld, left handed hitting
catcher also comes from the Bucs
to the Braves who were left with
Phil Mast as No. / receiver and the
only experienced major league
catcher on the club after they re-
leased Hank Camelli.
Veeck Seeks Two Brownies.


In exchange for their newcomers
the Sox have given up to the Browns
Infielders Eddie Pellagrini and Sam
Dente, Pitchers Glen Dreisewerd,
Jim Wilson and Al Widmar and
Outfelder Pete Layden, plus cash
and another player to be an
nounced.


Hardly had the deal bringing
Kinder and Utility Infielder Billy
Hitchcock to the Sox been an
nounced when Cleveland Indians
General Manager Bill Veeck said he
had offered the Browns more than
$75, 900 and two unidentified players
for Kinder and Pitcher Bob Num-
Grief.


To get Russell, Lyons and Salkeld
from the Pirates the Braves gave up
Outhelder Johnny Hopp, perhaps
one of the fastest men in baseball
who is left-handed all the way, and
Infielder Danny Murtaugh. The
latter spent last season with the
Milwaukee Brewers of the triple-A
American Association, Braves
farm.


The more rabid of the fans now
say "all we have to do to see the
neyt World Series Is travel about a
mile up and down Commonwealth
avenue between Fenway Park anG
Braves Field"

lean Power Boat Associations Water

like these in the English language to
describe clowns. Some of the terms
indicate the antiquity and universal
ity of the clowning profession.
"Zany" is the Greek word for clowns.
as used by Aristophanes. "Jocula-
tors" were Nero's buffoons who en-
tertained in the arena between acts.
while the guards went backstage for
a fresh batch of early Christians.


The present-day circus clown is
called "joey' in the show business
modem slang term. But the ruff
he wears was worn by Shakespeare's
merry-andrews, mimicking the fash
ion of the Elizabethan gallants. His
whitened face, his tight skullcap
reveal his debt to character called
Harlequin" invented in the year
1900. His slapstick came down from
earliest antiquity.

BOSTON, Oct. 9.-The CIO boy
colt of the National Labor Relations
Board was crumbling fast today.


The CIO convention here next
week is almost certain to avoid any
policy that would encourage con-
tinuation Of that boycott.


Instead. the convention will make
a strenuous attack on the Taft
Hartley labor law, but will state
that each of the Al CIO unions must
decide for itself whether to file COM
plants and petitions before the re.
organized NLRB under the new law.


Those facts became clear today
as leaders of the CIO held committee
meetings to prepare for the conven-
ton.


Convention Opens Monday.


Reporters learned that the top
officers of the CIO. president, Sec
retary- treasurer, and vice presidents,
came to an agreement last night on
the general substance of policy
statement on CIO use of the NLRB.


This agreement will go before the
52-member executive board tomor-
row, and then to the convention
which opens Monday.


The agreement was not formally
announced, but every indication was
that the CIO leadership could not
under the circumstances do, any
thing but leave each union free to
decide whether to provide the
necessary papers-including nom
Communist affidavits from its Off
cers-that will permit the filing OF
cases before the NLRB.
Privately CIO officials pointed out
that such a wide difference Of opin-
ion exists among CIO unions that
neither the board nor the. conven-
ton could very we'll attempt to
force either group to conform to a
! uniform policy.


13 Decide on Boycott.
About 13 unions, including the
right wing steel workers and the
left-wing electrical workers, have
decided to boycott the NLRB.
Or the other hand, four unions
have already filed the necessary
statements with the Government
and now are eligible to start cases
against employers for unfair labor
practices and to ask for bargaining
elections.


These are the textile workers,
woodWorkers, toyworkers and brew
cry workers. Many other CIO unions
are expected to take the same
course soon.

LAKE SUCCESS, July 11.-There
was $3.50 chance today that
France would take the initiative In
an attempt to reconcile the OPP
posed American and Russian pro-
posals for settlement of the Balkan
disorders.


Authoritative sources said Alex
andre Parodi, chief French dele
gate, might formally submit a COM
promise proposal when the United
Nations Security Council convened
this morning.


Despite American coolness to the
Parodi' proposal, which was dis
closed to the American delegation
in informal talks, these sources said
the French delegate had not de-
cided to shelve his compromise plan
Details Are Lacking.
The French plan was understood
to be designed to water down the
American resolution calling for a
semi mi-permanent investigation COM
mission to halt Greek border dis
turbances.


Details of the French proposal
were lacking, but it was reported to
call for commission without power
to act except with the express con-
sent of Greece and Russia's three
satellites-Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and
Albania.


The compromise wording would
give the commission power only to
help the government work out prob
lens of minorities, refugees and
border conventions.


The American delegation has
made it clear that it would settle
for nothing less than a commission
with power to handle the border
disputes and halt them.


Russia already has rejected the
commission idea, put all the blame
on Greece, and insisted that the
Athens government itself take steps
to correct the situation.


The Soviet Union suggested that
as q step toward clearing up the
situation all foreign troops should
be pulled out of Greece.


Since the Security Council did
not take up the Balkan question
yesterday, all hope of reaching a
vote on the issue today faded. Most
delegates, however, believed that
the Council would reach vote next
week.


Candidate Is Sought.


Meanwhile, the Security Council
failed again to reach any agree
nent on a candidate for the, gov
ernorship of Trieste.


At a closed session yesterday
Australia, Poland and Columbia
were named to collect information
about candidates already suggested
as we'll as other possible candidates" j."


Colombia submitted the names OF
four new candidates from Panama,
Chile, Peru and Mexico, which will
be considered by the three-2ation
committee.


The names of the new candidates
we're not disclosed, but there was
speculation in informed quarters
that they might include Manuel
Avila Camacho, former President OF
Mexico, and Ricardo Alfaro, former
President of Panama.

ATHENS, Oct. 22.-Press reports
said today that the Greek Army has
scheduled winter offensive against
the guerrillas to start November Is
when the current amnesty offer
expires, and that more than 100
villages in the Pindus and Hasia
mountains in the north have been
evacuated in preparation for the
push.

offensive were drawn in a recent
military meeting at Volos under
Craftsmanship of King Paul. Twenty
thousand new national guardsmen
will be charged with static defense
of the villages, freeing the army for
attacks in the Western Macedonian
mountains, they said.


A strong guerrilla force in military
uniforms and steel helmets was re-
ported to have attacked Edessa Mon
day night, looting a hospital and
abducting doctor, three nurses, two
gendarmes, 18 young men and seven
girls.

lea have been instituted, they said.

not know the origin of the threats,
but asserted they came to the off,
cial knowledge of the United States
Government.

September 3.

One point per pound of tuna

and crewmen were missing. Au-

charred hulk of the ship would give
up even more bodies as the search
was pressed. Scores of passengers
most of them Chinese, leaped over
board to escape the flames and some
of them may have drowned.


The Salon, which had been ply
ing between Hong Kong and Canton
was carrying highly inflammable
cargo of cotton and paper, and the
fire swept through the vessel with
terrifying rapidity. Many of the
steerage passengers were trapped
below decks.


Unofficial reports circulated thai
sabotage was involved in the fire
Sources preferring not to be identi-
fed said they understood the owners
of the Salon had received a threat
ening letter. They speculated that
terrorists blamed for 10 bombings OF
cafes, theaterS and gold shops here
in the last three months might be
resorting to diversionary tactics
Company officials could not be
reached for comment.

The Alexandria Hospital Board
today requested meeting with the
City Council to discuss a 1948 con-

The request is scheduled for con-

tomorrow night.

tiation.

meet with the council to outline

year.

discuss emergency room payments

contract was held in allegiance until
the number of "chargeable" emer-
gency patients could be determined

position on acquiring two war hous-

Chinquapin Village. The city heads
met with housing and home finance

preliminary discussion about the
two projects. The city has not yet
decided whether it would use the
two projects as low-rent housing for
veterans or favor continued use of
some sections of them by the Army
and Navy.

CHEYENNE, Wyo., Oct. "A decade ago
the political team Martha and Bob Taft
made big splash in Ohio Today the same
team, playing the national circuit, is making
the voters sit up and take notice. In 1888
Mrs. Taft stumped Ohio-all of it-for her
husband who was seeking the Republican sem
atorial nomination against organizations -sup-~
ported Arthur Day. 1t was tough fight which
Mr. Taft won. His next hurdle>was the election.
against Democratic Senator Bulkley, and with
the aid of Martha he won that too, although
the late President Franklin D. Roosevelt and
other top New Dealers threw everything they
had into the campaign for Mr.. Bulkley. Not a
little of the credit went to Mrs. Taft, and
rightly so.


As political speaker, Mrs. Taft stands out
among wonderland with women Mostly she
works the feminine side of the street, while
her husband, the Senator, sledge-hammers



excellent foil for the most serious pronounce
ments of Bob"


On the Western swing which the Tafts have
just completed Mrs Taft made three major
addresses to Republican women's organiza-
tions in as many States. and followed them up
with several brief talks, sometimes before
women and at other times before mixed gather
ings. Should Senator Taft win the Republican
presidential nomination. the second half OF the
Taft team will be much in demand during
the campaign.


Coined Slogan.


Speaking in Seattle, Mrs. Taft coined
slogan for the Republicans which already is
being seized upon: After next year, the only
fellow travellers around Washington will be
the fellows travelling away from Washington"


She has bite in her speeches, too. Explain-
ing why the Republican Congress was unable
during its last session to deal with public-Wel-
fare legislation, she said there hadn't been
sufficient time. Don't forget" she said, the
session opened with filibuster to seat Biloo
(the late Senator from Mississippi whose seat
ing Senator Taft opposed as Republican leader)
and ended with filibuster to cover up the
Kansas City vote scandals Every one knew
President Truman could have had an honest
investigation of those frauds If he had wished

administration and the Senate Democrats for
a stupid political play which left the country
suspecting that the President had much to
conceal about the vote scandals in his own
home State.


How Mrs Taft acquired her ability to make
political speeches is secret Of her own. She
admits she was interested in politics even
before she married Mr.. Taft. Her father,
the late Lloyd Bowers Of Michigan, was So
licitor General of the United States In the
administration of President William Howard
Taft He had been classmate at college OF
the President. In the natural course OF
events she met the younger Taft and they
were married soon after Mr.. Taft was gradu-
ated from the Harvard Law School. She did
rot really get into the political game, how
ever, until Mr.. Taft made his run Tor the
Senate While he was running for the State
Legislature, Mrs Taft was too busy with their
children and running home to take to the
stump.


Speaks With Ease.


She speaks with entire ease and without
notes, which gives her always q great adVan-
tage. She has, too. logical mind which car
ries her through to a successful elimination
Of her addresses When 1t comes to speaking
Of Republican principles, Republican accom-
plishmentse and the Republican program, she
is on her toes all the way She has, too.
way of humariAng an otherwise dry subject


Always running through her speeches is
the theme OF her faith In her husband. What
she says is to build him up-not herself-and
she does q swell job at it. And when she
appears on the same platform, her slogan Is:
Let him tell his story She sits and listens
with rapt attention, no matter how many
times she may have already heard the speech


Mrs. Taft, like her husband, takes things
as they come in political campaign She
was right beside Senator Taft In every case
on this Western trip when Senator Taft had
to cross labor union and Communist picket
lines Nor did she complain. Indeed, her
only comment after the most hostile Demon
stration Of them all, in Seattle was: Il don't
think they (the pickets) could have been
Communists really, for some of them grinned
at me-"


While she was campaigning in 1888 for her
husband she toured alone, often driving her
own car. On one occasion she ran off the
road into ditch to avoid a truck, and her
car overturned. She scrambled out, got .
farmer to drive her to the town where she
was to speak and filled her engagement.

All this, however, seems to conform to

greater contrast could be well imagined
between the political life of Ecuador and
that of Paraguay, where the inhabitants
seem to have a definite fondness for

Nevertheless, Ecuador is far from being
a terrestrial paradise. Inefficiency, graft,

Ecuador is relatively small country,

steaming tropical coast. The capital,
Quito, charming old Spanish colonial

The eastern half of the country, forming
part of the Amazon Basin, is thinly peopled,
undeveloped and only partially explored.

SALT LAKE CITY, July Is
Gov. Thomas E. Dewey of New
York won first place by a wide
margin today in a secret-ballot
poll of Republican Governors
expressing their preference for
the 1948 COP presidential
nominee.
Democratic Governors showed such
wide variance Of opinion in the
same, poll that only one potential
candidate got as many as two first
place votes for the vice presidential
nomination. He was former Secre-
tary of State James F. Byrnes.


In a poll conducted by the Asso-
ciated Press in cooperation with the
Deseret News and the Salt Lake Tel
egram, Gov. Dewey received 10 first
place votes and his nearest con-
tender, Gov. Earl Warren Of Cali
fornia, 2.


Democrats Undecided.
The remainder of the total Of II
first place votes cast by the Repub-
lican Governors were distributed one
each to Senator Taft of Ohio, former
Gov. Harold E. Stassen of Minnesota,
Gov. Dwight Green of Illinois, Sem
ator Saltonstall of Massachusetts,
and Senator Martin of Pennsylvania.


The indecision of Democrats
about a vice presidential runner
with President Truman was demon
strated by single tirst-place votes
for nine possible candidates, follow
ing the two for Mr. Byrnes.


This field included Secretary of
State Marshall, who addressed the
annual Governors Conference here
last night.


Others are Navy Secretary For
restal, Commerce Secretary Harri-
man, Gov. Mon Wangren of Wash
ington, Senator Lucas of Illinois,
Senator Byrd of Virginia, former
Gov. Robert S. Kerr of Oklahoma,
former Gov. Ellis Arnau of Georgia
and Senator O'Mahoney of Wyo-
ming.


II Republicans Vote.


To insure freedom of expression,
reporters for the. Associated Press,
the News and the Telegram asked
Governors to write their preferences
on unmarked slips of paper which
could not be identified when the
boxes were opened.


Seventeen Republican Governors
and II Democrats participated in the
poll out of the 43 State executives
now present at the conference
Others either did not participate or
said they had not made up their
minds.


Mr.. Stassen, the only publicly
announced candidate for the COP
presidential nomination, topped the
list of second choices with 6 of
the Is Republican votes in that
bracket. Senator Vandenberg of
Michigan and Senator Bricker of
Ohio made their first appearance
in the poll with two second choice
votes each. Senator Taft also got
the same number.


One second choice vote each was
cast for Gen. Macarthur, House
Speaker Martin of Massachusetts,,
Gov. Dewey and Gov. Warren.


Strangely enough, Gov. Warren
was top man in the third choice
bracket with nine votes. Speaker
Martin got two and Dewey, Stassen,
Vandenberg and Green one each.


Eisenhower Gets Ballot.


Gen. Eisenhower's name appeared
in the poll for the first time with
one third choice vote.


Counting all Of the first, second
and third place votes. Dewey and
Warren topped the list with IL
each. Stassen got eight, Taft, Van
denberg and Speaker Martin, three
each, and Bricker and Green, two
each.
On the Democratic side. Byrnes,
Hartman, Lucas and Byrd were
the only ones who accumulated
two votes each in the three classi-
fications.


Interior Secretary Krug, Justice
William o. Douglas. Minority Lead
er Barley of Kentucky, Senator
Tydings of Maryland, former Gov.
Colgate Darden of Virginia and
Gov. Herbert Nav Of Utah were
listed among those who got one
second-choice vote.


Former Gov. Frank Lausche OF
Ohio and former Gov. Prentice
Cooper of Tennessee got one third
choice vote each.


The Governors balloting ran
strongly to State executives, includ-
ing some Senators and other officiels
who served as Governors before they
undertook other duties


The preferences they expressed, 1t
was made plain, were their per-
sonal choices and not necessarily
representative of their States polit-
ical views.
