oughly the past year as GSI. The Baldwin
subcommittee of the Senate Civil Service
Committee has peered into virtually every
corner of the sprawling, Government
sponsored but essentially private corpora
ton. At the request of the subcommittee
the Federal Bureau of Investigation has
examined records of the lengthy hearings.
The Controller General has audited GSIs
books.


The FBI reported that it could find no
evidence of law violation to warrant fur
ther investigation by its agents. The Con-
troller General, while finding room for
Improvement in some phases of GSI oper-
alton, stated that, in general, the agency'S
affairs had been we'll conducted. And now
the worst that the Baldwin Subcommittee
has been able to find wrong with GSI is
what it terms its "loose management"


Even GSI's most ardent supporters had
never contended that its management has
been beyond criticism at all times, how
ever Mistakes have been made and ad-
mitted. But perfect management could
hardly have been expected, in view OF war
born problems which were thrust upon
Manager Hoover and his staff. The rapid
expansion of Government personnel which
took place between 1941 and 1945 required
a like expansion of cafeteria and welfare
services. The agency has grown until 1t
now comprises one hundred and thirty
units During the past twenty years 1t has
done a gross business of more than one
hundred million dollars. Last year alone
it crossed more than twelve million dollars.

Baldwin Subcommittee suggest that Con-
gress should consider reorganization OF
the existing trustee arrangement, under
which a group of Federal officials super
vises the management of GSI. The pur-
pose of this would be to separate the
policy making and administrative func-
tions. The Controller General also sees
the need for more clearly defined contracts
to avoid misunderstanding as to the limits
of responsibility of GSI and the Public
Buildings Administration in the equipment
field. These and several other proposed
reforms probably would improve GS1. To

of sensational charges made by critics OF

STATE COLLEGE, Pa. Oct. 25.-
Penn States powerful football team
remained among the unbeaten today

Virginia eleven, 21-14, for its fifth
straight victory.


A capacity crowd of $4,000 watched

faltered.

opening minutes of the first period

of lit yards on 16 plays.


Elwood Petchel, with two success

on West Virginia's 81 was another
sparkplug for the Lions, while Clar-
ence Gorinski, another sophomore,
plunged over from the 3 for the tying
tally in the closing minutes of the
second period.


Petchel pitched a pass to Wallace
Triplett that started on the West
Virginia At, was caught on the 26,
and the fleet Lion back swept along
to the tally that meant victory for
Penn State.


West Virginia's finest work came
in the opening period with an aerial
attack resulting in both its touch
downs. The first came when Tony
Keane tossed to Rex Bumsardner
on the State 26 and the referee
called pass interference on the play.
A few moments later the same pair
repeated and again interference was
called, this time on States 4. Pete
Zinaich plunged over for the touch
down.

burdened Red Troops marched

into Red strongholds in Shansi
province

Peiping Hankow railroad. The

towns northeast of the railtown of

scribed as most critical" the situa-
ton at the government base of

towns within six miles of Loyang.

NEW YORK, Sept. 1.-The whole
outdoor entertainment industry,
from pitchmen to popcorn whole
salers, have stiff necks from watch
ing the skies and crossed fingers
for luck as the United States fair
and carnival season reaches the
halfway mark.


With around half of the Nations
5000 scheduled county, district and
State fairs already over and done
with, the industry is hoping that
from now until early October they
can make up earlier losses.


Rainy skies and muddy fair
grounds, followed by intense and
burning heat, whitfield the business
down to shoestring operations. Gus
toners were notable by their alb
sence.


Weather Is Important.


Veterans of the fair and carnival
business predict few good weeks
ahead-weather permitting. Bumper
crops mean happy farmers; smoking
factory chimneys mean full en-
ployment. Together they produce
gay, free-spending crowds on the
midways of the Nations fair
grounds.


Fairs are big business in dollars
and in personnel. All through the
warm months gangs of laborers
from coast to coast are leveling
fields, ack-topping dusty acres and
erecting temporary grandstands,
stalls and booths.


Popcorn is selling for around $40
for 100 pounds; balloons are whole
sailing at 50 gross in the giant
size. There's . steady demand for
the usual stomach ache inducers,
led by candy floss, apple sticks,
French fries and ice cream in vari-
GUS forms and colors.


Better Prizes Demanded.
With items scarce during the war
years returning to retail store
shelves, fair patrons are demanding
better goods in prize awards and
merchandise. Merchandise found
in bigger machines"-called "slow''
by the trade-has to be more at
tractive. Flash merchandise" which
Is the better stuff shown as come
ons In the prize award games, gets
better returns when the still-scarce
items are well up front among the
displays.


Customers are showing strong
resistance to paying 10 cents a card
in the games Of chance along the
Bingo lines and the trade is in the
middle of a hot debate whether to
drop back to the prewar nickel price.


On the straight entertainment
side. there is continued popularity
for the old tried and true auto and
harness races, animals acts, aero
bats, girl shows. wire walking. knife
throwing, animal trainers, midgets.
fortune telling, merry-go-rounds
and the rest of the familiars.
Rivalry Helps Business.


Local participation and friendly
rivalries are an important part of
all the fairs and are growing more
important with the years. The All
clubs and women's groups spend
lavishly of time and effort to pro-
duce the best displays and contests
The Middle West and Southwest
are the gold mines for the profess
sionals, for the agricultural States
turn up the biggest crowds. Some
county fairs are held on the out
skirts of the big cities, but these are
rather elf-conscious affairs where
the carnival part predominates.


And then. when the amusement
parks and the fairs are all through
for another seven months, the trade
hopefully takes stock and prepares
for the biggest, best season of his
| tory: Next year.

The Interstate Commerce Commission
has shown proper regard for the public
interest in suspending proposed bus-fare
increase by the Washington, Virginia and
Maryland Coach Company, pending
thorough study of the rate proposal. Nearly
everybody but the bus company has evi-
denced vigorous opposition to fare raise,
but until the ICC took hand there was no
single forum before which merits of the
plan could be effectively debated.


The ICC is the only public utility agency
which has the authority necessary to deal
with an interstate question of this kind
Yet the problem of fares on purely local
buslines that come under Federal juris-
diction only because they happen to cross
the Districts boundaries regularly is one
with which some Metropolitan Area util-
tiles commission should be concerned 1t
is doubtful If the authors of the interstate
commerce laws ever contemplated that
the ICC would have to interest itself in
Washingtons suburban buslines. Yet it
has even been asked to fix taxicab rates
to Arlington and other nearby points.


But for the ICC, however, there would
be no authority to which citizens and
utilities could appeal IN these short-line
local cases. Arlington County's Public
Utilities Commission is a creation of the
County Board and has only advisory
powers. The Virginia Corporation Com
mission has only intrastate Jurisdiction.
The District Public Utilities Commission
has no control over fares charged across
the Potomac River. The Arlington County
Board, the Civic Federation and the pro-
testing customers of the Arnold lines car
ried their pleas to the ICC when it seemed
likely that the proposed fare raise was
to go into effect without public hearing
before any official body.


The Star believes there should be some
public utilities agency for the Metropolitan
Area which could devote It's attention
solely to the constantly arising rate and
service controversies involving bus and
taxicab lines operating within the area
An interstate compact among the District
OF Columbia, Maryland and Virginia might
provide the basis for setting up such an
agency. The need for some special COM
mission of this sort will become increas
lngly felt as the Metropolitan Areas trans
portation problems continue to grow.

GREEN PEAFOWL.


All history of peafowl Is clouded
in mystery. Their ancestry Is un-
known. Though these birds have
been familiar to mankind ever since
the Phoenicians brought them a.
gifts to the proud Egyptian Pha-
raohs, they have not changed in
form or habits since that ancient day.


All are handsome birds. Ths
males wear brilliant metallic plumags
with an amazing development Of the
lower back feathers. These are cov-
cred with pigmented eyes and form
an enormous train.


Green peafowl range over Burma,
Chittagong, Siam, Cochin China,
Malay Peninsula and Java. The male
has high, narrow-vaned crest. The
facial skin is blue and yellow. The
head and throat are green, with the
neck and forepart of body above and
below bronze with blue centers show
ing on the mantle His green back
is centered with bronze, edged with
blue. The posterior ventral surface
Is dull green and black. The
smaller wing coyerts show the same
shade Of green and the larger coverts
and primaries are chestnut. The
green train has many large oceln
(eyes) each ringed with bronze and
blue. His mates resemble him with
the exception that their upper body
plumage lacks the green gloss and
all plumage Is mottled with buff.
Perfect plumage is worn in June,
July and August, their courting
months.


To some extent, peafowls are the
most sedentary of birds. They rank
high mentally, not for keenness Of
senses, but adaptability. Unless
drought overtakes them, they remain
at home During courting days they
penetrate deeper into the jungle.
Aside from these departures, they
remain in a small area. They dine
regularly, quench their thirst at spe-
cial places and times Of the day and
retire promptly after dusk.


In the jungles they share identical
hazards with their neighbors, yet
remain the most abundant Of any
members of their family. They are
fearless, preferring to face ap-
preaching danger Father than run.
At times they take to the air. Their
sharp spurs make ugly wounds.
Nature gave peafowls beautiful
raiment, but withheld q musical
voice. Their loud powerful scream
is readily recognized.


The ridiculous swagger and stiff
legged strut, often mistaken for
showoff, is an attempt to keep the
train in the air and the owner on
his feet.

flower petals, worms, small lizards,
insects, grubs, frogs and even snakes
vary their remarkable menu. In
some spots they wipe out termite
nests. In some places peafowl are

LANSFORD, Pa, Feb. 15.-Claim-
ing victory in a fight over docked
pay, 13 weary and grimy anthracite
miners today ended a sitdown strike
which had kept them 800 feet under
ground nearly three days.


The bedraggled band. apparently
none the worse for the long siege,
walked out Of Lehigh Navigation
Coal Company's Lansford colliery
after management pledged to pay
wages deducted for failure to work
a full day.


The strike led to a general SYM
pathy work stoppage by 5000 dig
gers in the company's Panther
Valley mines, which produce 5000
tons Of coal daily. United Mine
Workers officials expected action
during the week end to permit quick
resumption of operations.


Chairman Fred Gallagher of the
Lansford colliery union committee
said the agreement provided that
consideration miners" such as the
sitdowners, will work full time here
after or arrange with officials for
shorter hours in event of abnormal
conditions.


Pay Fluctuates.


Consideration miners, who develop
new areas in the pits, are paid on
a production basis until the going
becomes too hard, then draw fiat
pay of SOTO daily.


The sitdowners claimed heat
smoke and dust prevented them put
ting in full time without endanger-
ing their health. They struck on
grounds that pay had been docked
as much as $50 in some cases. The
company said it wanted miners to
live up to their contract.


The sitdowners heard the scom-
,pany offer during three-hour cen
ference with UNIV District ~Presi-
dent Martin F. Brennan in the 40
by-20-foot mine chamber which they
had made home since Wednesday
night. Then the haggard, unshaven
group came to the surface.


"I would have stayed there until
Easter If necessary" declared one.
/ Men Rush Home.


After sleeping on benches during
the long stay in the cold, damp
gangways, the men headed for home
and bed. Steve Nemeth rushed to
his wife who is expecting baby.


Mr.. Gallagher said both the sit
downers and other miners appeared
pleased with the company offer. One
striker declared, ''It was just set
tlement. That's what we wanted"


The sitdown was the first such
portest in the eastern Pennsylvania
anthracite fields since 1887, when A
diggers stayed 1900 feet under
ground for week in a wage dispute

The Municipal Court Of Appeals passed

record of performance in which both Its
judges and the community may we'll take
pride.


This court reviews cases from all branches
OF the Municipal Court, from the Juvenile
Court and, through the Municipal Court,
from the local rent administrator. The
thought OF It's sponsors was that it would
expedite the handling of these cases and
take much of the load of the United States
Court of Appeals. That the tribunal has
fulfilled these expectations is shown by
some of its statistics.


Over the flve-year period it has had six
hundred and eighty yf1ye appeals submitted
and has dealt with seven hundred and
eighty-four motions OF various kinds. The
average elapsed time between the noting
Of an appeal in the trial court and final
decision in the appellate court has been
ninety-two days. The average elapsed time
between the date. of argument and final
decision has been thirty-one: Gays. AS OF
last Wednesday, there were only six cases
which had been heard and were still un-
decided


The municipal appellate court has been
reversed only nine times in five years by
the United States Court OF Appeals. Dur
ing that period there were one hundred
and thirteen applications to the United
States Court for reviews. Only twenty
three of these were granted, and the
municipal appellate court was sustained In
fourteen.


This is a record which reflects very
creditably on the work of Chief Judge
Cayton and his associates, Judges Hood
and Clagett.

Maj. Gen. Norman T. Kirk, Army
surgeon general, will formally open
the Army's new aural rehabilitation
center at Walter Reed Hospitals
Forest Glen section at 8 o'clock this
afternoon.


The new center will consolidate
all the Army's facilities for provid-
ing deaf servicemen with hearing
aids. In the past, GIs with hearing
defects have been centered for final
rehabilitation instruction at general
hospitals in Santa Barbara, Calf;
Chickasha, Okla, and Butler, Pa.


More than 200 servicemen are at
Forest Glen now taking part in the
program. according to Col. Guy A.
Owsley of Hartford City, Ind, direc-
tor Of the center. All of them, he
said, have completed medical treat
ment and will soon return to civilian
life.


The center itself was formerly
spacious Forest Glen cowbarn, Col.
Owsley said, that had been con-
verted to a unit of soundproof rooms,
lecture halls, laboratories and offices.


Latest developments in aural
training installed at the center in
clude courses in lip-reading and
speech correction. During the eight
week course, patients defects will
be closely analyzed to determine
how they can best be corrected.
About so technicians and instruc-
tors will assist Col. OWsley in the
work, he said.


The center will also have its own
laboratory to exactly fit hearing aids
with individual ear molds, the
director explained.

HELSIEKI, Finland, April IL
The government of Premier Mauno
Pakkala resigned today in what was
described here as purely domestic
political crisis engendered by Fin
lands postwar economic problems.


Mr.. Pekkala became Premier
March "a, 1916, succeeding Juho K
Paasikivi, who resigned to assume
the presidency The Pekkala govern
ment was a coalition of the three
largest political parties, with the
Communist-d o min a tee Peoples
Democratic Union holding six
cabinet posts, the Social Democrats
and Agrarians, five each, and the
Swedish Peoples Party, one.


The government and the Premier
were believed to have enjoyed the
full confidence of the Soviet Union.


The crisis arose from almost two
months of dissension over an eco
nomic stabilization program, culmi-
mating last week in demands from
the Peoples Democratic Union for
abandonment of controls over wages
plus sharpening of price control.


Authoritative sources expressed
fear that the crisis might cause
misunderstanding abroad, and en-
phasized that the resignation had
no connection with the forthcoming
ratification Of the Finnish peace
treaty.

ment store, largest retail establish
ment in this South Island city.

knock you come in" After sew
eral minutes there was no knock

found their brothers body hang

boy. Police notified Joey's parents

peace conference. had virtually
promised that the frontiers would
be changed.

SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct. 15.-A A
government spokesman said today
that Defense Minister Gen. Guiller-
mo Barros Tirado had reported
from the Chilean coal fields that
striking coal miners were disobeying
government back-to-work order
because they feared Communist
secret police organization.

called the secret police organiza-
ton "Cheka," one of the names
given the Russian secret police.


He announced that any members
of such an organization found keep
ing coal miners away from work
would be transported with their
families away from the coal fields.


The strike of 5000 coal miners,
which the government blames on
Communist agitation, entered its
18th day today, despite determined
government efforts to end it. The
miners say they want more pay and
the government says it has offered
wage increases of 80 to 40 per cent.

ROME, sept. 20.-Reports from
throughout Italy tonight said the
Communist and Socialist inspired
great day of manifestation" against
economic conditions under Premier
Alcide de Gasperi's Christian Dem
ocrat government had passed quietly
and, in some cities, met with in
difference.


Most cities reported that crowds
which gathered at afternoon mass
meetings were smaller than expected


The audiences gathered quietly
and listened without much response
to speakers from several leftist
parties denounce the government,
then furled their red banners and
Italian flags, put their placards
bearing anti-government slogans
under their arms and, just as quietly
went home.


In frequently turbulent Naples.
the crowd of about 10000 began
to disperse before the final speaker
took the stand.


Little Excitement at Meetings.


In the leftist industrial cities of
Genoa, Milan and Florence there
was no excitement, although the
mass meetings attracted as many
as 100000.


Notably absent from speakers
platforms were Italian communism's
big guns, Palmiro Togliatti and
Luigi Longo, as well as pro-Com-
munist Socialist Leader Pietro
Nenni.


The orderly and placid gather
ings were contrary to expectation
after several government spokesman
had declared the demonstrations
were aimed at overthrow of the
government and Togliatti had as
serted the country was largely ripe
for revolution. Police precautions
against violence were light.


The Roman demonstrators carried
plaeards blaming the Christian
Democratic government for eco
.nomic ills.


Five Parties Represented.


1--WE are tired of a government
which protects spectators, hunger
for all or hunger for none this
eovernment-is it democratic? Is
it Christian?," the placards said.


Today's demonstrations occurred
on the anniversary of the end of
Vatican rule of the papal states in
1870, a date of anticlerical signif1-
canoe in Italian history.

cars, backed up with heavy forces
of mobile and mounted police carry
ing tommyguns, surrounded Left
Wing gatherings. Only light forces
of ordinary police were visible today
and. they carried only their usual
arms.

CADIz, Spain, Aug. 21.- The
Provincial Board of Health, giving
the first official casualty figures for
Monday nights arms blast in Cadiz
said today $50 persons were known
to have perished and about 80
bodies remained beneath the wreck
age.


The board said the number Of in
jured totaled approximately 5000,
including $50 seriously hurt. Sew
eral thousand persons, the board
added. suffered cuts and bruises
from flying glass and debris.
Mayor Francisco Sanchez CoSsio
estimated earlier that the death
toll from the shattering explosion at
the nearby naval torpedo and mine
factory would reach approximately
200.


Mayor Sanchez appealed to Gen
eraHssimo Franco today to remove
armament and munition stores re-
naming within the city limits, say
ing they were liable to cause fur
ther disaster.


In note handed to Rear Ad-
miral Francisco Delgado, the navy
minister, to be relayed to Gen.
Franco, the mayor also outlined the
urgent reconstruction problems fac
ing the city.


He stressed problems of housing,
employment and business resulting
from the blast damage, which early
estimates said would pass 100000
900. He requested early considera-
ton for repairs to business buildings
and to the city's main streets in
the heart of Cadiz, practically all
of which suffered some damage.


Mayor Sanchez also asked the
generalissimo to rebuild the old-age
home, hospitals, maternity home
and other public institutions de-
stroyed by the blast. He empha-
sized industrial problems such as
those at the ravaged Echevarrieta
and Labrinaga shipyards, which are
especially important to the economy
of Cadiz.


He appealed especially for gov
ernment moratorium for commerce
and industry in Cadiz.


Most of Cuba's avocado crop will
come to the United States by air

Shows $50 Dead, 80
Missing in Cadiz Blast

nounced in Asuncion last night that

capital said no firing had been

nounced yesterday the capture OF
the rebels river merchant boats

from Conception down the Para
quay River for the attack on Ascun-
cion. The boats surrendered un-
conditionally and put into Asun-
cion's port. the announcement said.

ton of the two rebel gunboats, the
Paraguay and the Humaita, which
last were reported in the Parana
River in the south. Previous reports

interned by Argentine authorities,

NEW YORK, Feb. 1.-Forty panic
stricken passengers, all but two OF
whom we're hurt, fought their way
out of blazing Brooklyn trolley
car last night. Mothers smashed
windows and handed their children
to persons outside.


Two men ran from a restaurant
and finally opened the car doors.
The doors were stuck when the
power went off.


The car was operated by woman,
Eva Rollings, colored. Police said
she would not leave the car until
all the passengers were out.


Twenty mine persons were treated
at the scene by ambulance doctors.
Nine others were taken to Kings
County Hospital suffering from cuts,
shock and smoke poisoning, but
police said their condition was not
serious.


The car was passing through a
busy shopping section when oc-
cupants first heard a loud noise
and then saw flames and smoke
mushrooming around the sides.
Shortly the flames burst through
the floor. The car stopped, the
lights went out and the doors re-
fused to open.


Police blamed the flash fire on .
short circuit in the fuse box. Trafie
was stopped for a half hour.

rier. Rolling down the ramp and

ground organization, Immediately

TRIESTE, Sept. 20. - The
American destroyer Douglas H.
Fox struck a mine 18 miles off
Trieste this afternoon as she was
heading for this free territory.


Three men were killed, according
to a message from the destroyer
J. c. Owen. which went to the
Fox's rescue. Naval headquarters
here earlier had reported one dead,
and it was assumed that two of
the injured men had died.


The Owen reported she was bring
ing In 10 litter cases and two walk
ing wounded. The Fox had COM
plement of about 200 men.


Two tugs were sent to escort the
Fox to Venice, only nearby port
equipped with a drydock. The Fox
was en- route from Venice to Trieste
when she hit the mine.


The Navy said here that the mine
exploded the destroyer, wrecking
the steering gear and flooding all the
after compartments. The Fox was
one of the newest type warships.

Navy officials said the mine may
have been an old one, broken loose
from an area pot yet swept clear
since the war.


The names of the victims were not
made public at once.


The Fox, which was on her way
from Venice, Italy. to Trieste, Is one
of the most heavily armed of Amer
ican destroyers. Her main battery
carries six 5-inch guns plus 10 tor
pedo tubes. She joined the United
States warships in the Mediter-
ranean after leaving Norfolk, Va,
July 81.

A Sumner class destroyer, the Fox
was built in 1914, displaces 1900

shoot them.

other headquarters where they were
met by "a very friendly" major.


The major sent them still further
into Yugoslavia where they were
interrogated twice. They said they
were given good food and good beds
and were not molested further.


British sources said they expected
a strong" official protest would
not be made concerning the case.

Frightened residents boarded up
homes and business buildings
along the Gulf Coast of Western
Florida before an advancing
hurricane, and Gov. Millard
Caldwell's office announced that
President Truman had declared
a state of emergency in Florida
> The announcement came few
hours after the Weather Bureau dis
closed that the treacherous tropical
storm had curved sharply after in
f1icting multi-million dollar damage
on Southern Florida, and was head
ed back toward the western main
land from the Gulf of Mexico.


Yesterday the hurricane ripped a
path of destruction across Florida S
most famous playground and farm
ing section. 1t roared inland with
l20-lnile winds between Miami and
Palm Beach and emerged into the
Gulf near Fort Myers with scarcely
diminished velocity.


60 Miles Off Tampa Bay.

storm roughly so miles off the mouth
of Tampa Bay at 1890 pm. (EDT)
and forecasts indicated it would
slam into the low-lying Western
Florida about midnight, between
Pensacola and Apalachicola. Hur-
ricane flags flew from Pensacola
to st. Marks, and winds up to 100
m.p.h. we're anticipated.


Civilians in the danger area were
being moved to reinforced buildings
and beach residents fled to town.
Seven Cuban fishing boats landed at

beach homes rushed from the capi-

Mr.. Truman's emergency procla-

Administration to distribute relief
supplies in all hurricane areas.

night diminished to gale strength
today, but continued to hamper
transportation and communication.

Baak announced that credits would
be extended to finance replacement
Of storm damaged property and
would be exempt from usual con-
sumer-credit controls.

Folsom offered aid to Florida. and
ordered II Alabama highway patrol
men into the threatened storm area
for disaster duty. The Red Cross
and other agencies braced for the
newest blow.

cola west to Mobile, and heavy
weather was expected east of Apal-
achee Bay.


The damaging hurricane, which
yesterday whipped the rich resort
and agricultural areas of South

its course abruptly after entering
the gulf near Fort Myers last night.
Early reports indicated it might
move westward without further
menace to land, but it began to wal

with accelerated speed.


The tropical disturbance, the
worst experienced by Florida in a
decade. left at least two dead
thousands of emergency sheltered
refugees, and II stranded or missing

OLYMPUS, Mar. 1.-Two cyclonic
cradles, where storms are produced
affecting most Of the world south
of the equator, have been discov-
cred by meteorologists on this ex-
pedition. .


One is on the polar plateau near
the South magnetic pole. Here
cold air sweeps northward from
the South Pole itself. This air
crashes into warm north winds
somewhere near the Balleny Islands,
creating cyclones which turn east
ward and gather force rapidly over
the Ross Sea.


The other cradle is near Mount
Ruth Siple, on the western edge
of the Roosevelt Sea. Cold air,
sweeping through q wide gap in
the mountains, again meets warm
north winds. Cyclones from this
cradle finally collapse somewhere
over the Palmer Peninsula.


Science thus can account for the
origin Of storms In two of the four
quadrants into which Antarctica Is

why do they weep then, and why

LONDON, Feb. 15.-Australia

in occupied Germany.


In a new note to the Big Four

not yet proved herself fit for demo-
cratic self government and existing
control machinery was unsuitable.


"The Allied Control Council lacks
full Allied sanction, = denying
substantial belligerents any share
in the controls" the note said.


Australia proposed policy-mak-
ing body to guide the Allied Control
Council and said all smaller allies
in the category of active belligerents
should have membership.


The note did not ask that smaller
nations provide troops for the oc-
cupation.


No Sympathy for Germans.


The Australian government said
1t did not wish to extend sympathy
to the Germans" but felt they
should be allowed a higher level
of prosperity to help "the growth
of genuine democratic forces" and
prevent "the resurgence OF Fascism.' y


Opposing any rigid rules" estab-
fishing Germany as union fedora

would replace Poland, Australia and
Brazil, whose terms expire Jan. /.

cept or whether Russia wanted the
Prague government as the second
member from Eastern Europe. Rus

eminent for the place.


For the 18-nation economic and
Social Council, where the terms of
Russia, Britain, Cuba, Czechoslo-
vakia, India and Norway expire,
the American delegation was re-
ported ready to back Russia and
Britain for reelection and Iran,
Poland, Denmark and Brazil as new
members.


The Trusteeship Council also has
to name two additional members
and the leading choices were the
Philippines and Norway.


Elections for the Security and
Economic and Social Councils will
be held by secret ballot without
nominations in plenary session
of the General Assembly at Flush
ing


The United States, Russia, France,
Britain and China hold permanent
seats on the 11-nation Security
Council The other six members
are elected for two-year terms with
three expiring every January l..

vakia and Canada be elected next
week, they would hold seats Janu-
ary l along with the Big Five, and
Colombia, Syria and Belgium-the
three members whose terms still
have year to run.


Terms on the Economic and Social
Council run for three years with
q third of the 18-nation council be-
ing replaced every year. To create
the system of rotation and vary the
expiration dates, The U. N. elected
for one, two and three years when

in the weather.

nent and the British Isles reported

December l.

grees lower than normal. Air Min
istry forecasters predicted even
lower temperatures would follow
clearing skies and said the long
range outlook was for very cold
conditions continuing"

TO the EDITOR OF tne star:


While we here in Washington get out
our heaviest coats and extra blankets
to combat the coolest days and nights of
winter, countless thousands abroad have
neither coats nor blankets to protect
them from the bitter weather. More
than that, they often have no shelter
that properly could be called home.
1t is more than difficult for us to realize
all that is meant when we speak of
conditions abroad"


But little imagination can paint
picture that will help. Think of your
house some night next week with the
glass gone from the windows, the doors
closed only with pieces of cardboard,
the wind blowing in through every
crack. Then put out the lights, sit in
the dark as though you could have no
electricity. Picture your family living
in q corner Of q cellar. Consider that
the clothes you have on are the only
ones you own, and that only your shoes
keep your feet from the bare ground.
That's how winter feels to millions in
Europe and Asia right now. And that's
why the clothing drive beginning in
Washington this week Is most important.


Nearly every family here has stored
away In closets and drawers clothing
they never use, warm clothing. things
that others could wear; suits that are
outgrown, dresses and sweaters not worn
any longer, shoes, childrens clothing,
overshoes and rubbers. Your old felt
hats can be made into slippers for a
Chinese child; your old tablecloth,
diapers for an Austrian baby; your worn
blanket, decked with a patchwork
covering, could warm the hearts and
bodies of refugee family.


Gather up your extra clothing and call
Dupont 1478 for the address OF the
collection center nearest you.


RUTH A. ELLIOTT.

Representative Hebert's surprise
and evident irritation over the
eleventh-hour appeal direct to Con-
gress against the already started
Dupont Circle underpass plan are
understandable. What are the last
minute discoveries which justify the
belated hue and cry by some civic
and business interests against a
highway project which has been
under discussion for about ten years
and which previously has received
widespread public approval?


The Dupont Circle underpass has
been threshed out from every con-
ceivable angle during the years that
it has been in the planning stage.
Such questions as whether an under
pass was necessary at all, whether
the tunnel should follow the line of
Massachusetts or Connecticut ave-
nues, how the streetcar tracks should
be handled, how best to preserve
the beauty of the circle and how to
minimize interference with business
In the vicinity were discussed at
public hearings and studied by high
way, traffic and park experts. Among
those who have formally Endorsed
the plan as finally adopted are the
Connecticut Avenue Association,
composed of business interests, the
Dupont Circle Citizens Association
and the National Capital Park and
Planning Commission.


There has been no secrecy about
any phase of the operation. The
general design has been published
in the newspapers. bids have been
advertised for preliminary work and
actual construction has been under
way for some weeks. Yet joint
House-Senate subcommittee found
itself besieged with citizens alleging
various things, including claims that
the cost will run too high and that
business will be hurt if the under
pass is built. Committee members,
are justified in their criticism of
such last-minute appeals by citizens
who had ample opportunity tosvcice,,
protests to the Commissioners earlier
but failed to do so.


If new situations have arisen
which require halting of the project
at this late date and a review of
the plans. the discoverers of these
new situations should take their case
not to the Capitol but to the District
Building. Unless the hew informa-
ton is more persuasive than that
unfolded to the joint committee last
week, however. there seems to be no
good reason for further delaying
the important Dupont Circle traffic
acceleration program.

F'orsythia was named for William
FORSYTH, a well-known English hor-
tuculturist, director of the Royal
Garden at Kensington.


Forsythia, known also as golden
bells, is one of the favorite shrubs
in America. Even in February one
NAV 20 out and cut some OF the
branches for the house. Warm tenn
perature and water soon coax the
buds to swell and finally the entire
branch is laden with lovely golden
bells.


These Towering shrubs have
beautiful dark green foliage. The
opposite leaves arrive after the oloS-
SONS have almost gone. In the
early spring the shrub glows with a
profusion of yellow blossoms. some
times in such profusion the limbs
bend to the ground with their golden
treasure. The forsythia is a show
off. For landscaping 1t Is an ideal
shrub. The upright forms are more
suited for borders of shrubberies.
The pendulous form for decorating
and in some cases hiding fences and
unsightly spots. They are excellent
for porches where privacy is desired.
The leaves are dark green, clean
and glossy. They are remarkably
free from insects and fungi, remain
ing in fine condition throughout the
summer and late autumn. There
are four species in China, Japan and
Southeastern Europe.


Almost any kind Of soil Is accept
able. Being hardy, the shrubs make
the best of every situation. Given
attention, they become glorious
fountains of golden bells in the early
spring.

ROME ANTARCTIC BASE,
Marguerite Bay. Nov. 4 Delayed i.
-Comdr Finn Rome and his party
left this bese by air today for ad-
vanced exploration base at Capt
Keeler on the Weddell Sea Coast
Depending on the weather. the
miniature city which has sprung
up there soon will be moved by
air still farther south on the east
side of the Palmer Peninsula,
whence exploratory flights will fan
out to map the hitherto unexplored
sections of the Weddell Sea Coast
last stretch still unmapped around
this vast continent.


The weather has seriously delayed
the entire operation. For weeks,
overcast had kept the planes
grounded at the main base. Today's
clear weather was only momentary
but was Immediately seized upon
to get the two heavily loaded planes,
the Ed Sweeney" and the Mana"
off the ground. The weasel had
packed the snow on the runway,
but the heavy loads and the absence
of wind made several taxing runs
necessary.


Eventually Capt. James Lassiter
and Comdr. Rome left in the
Beechcraft Ed Sweeney" with full
load of gasoline and field equipment
as well as the three trimetrogon
aerial mapping cameras and $50
pounds of film. 1t Charles Adams
and Photographer William Latady
left in the Mana" with more gaso-
line and field equipment. Both
pilots had hoped to return to the
main base today. as they had yes
terday, to take on additional fuel
and cargo and to pick up Mechanic
James Robertson, but the overcast
closed In again as soon as the planes
had left. making additional landings
here today impossible.


Capt. Lassiter and 1t. Adams each
made round trip to Cape Keeler
yesterday, leaving Comdr. Isaac
Schlossbach there. The base al
ready has taken on considerable life,
they reported on their return. Nu-
merous small tentS~and igloos dot
the white surface of the area.


Before the pilots left yesterday the
joint British american sledge party
pulled into camp after their long
overland haul, They plan to leave
at midnight tonight for Cape
Knowles and Mount Tricorn. Navi-
gator Walter Smith will replace
Physicist Andrew Thompson in the
sledge party, continuing south with
Boy Scout Arthur Owen and the
two Britons.

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. 1.-Two
long touchdown passes, thrown by
Clyde Leforce from near midfield,
provided the winning scores for the
Western All-Stars in the 22d annual
Shrine charity classic played before
1000 football fans at Kezar Stadi-
um New Year Day. The West won,
1879.


Taking advantage of the fast, dry
field and clear weather, both teams
quickly abandoned any ideas they
might have had Of depending on
running plays and resorted to wide
open passing offensives throughout
the game. What little running was
done was mainly to open up oppos-
ing defenses.


The East, with Nick Sacrinty en-
gineering its air attack in spectacu-
lar fashion, had q small edge for
three quarters but, when the Wake
Forest star was hurt in the last Pc
riod, the West went on to win. And
It was Leforce, the Tulsa University
ace, who made the difference. ~.


Sacrinty had no more than limped
to the sidelines than Leforce threw
q long, low pass to Gene Wilson,
Methodist University's fine
end. to wipe out a 3-point Eastern
lead and win the hard-fought game.
Wilson took the ball on the dead
run and went 80 yards to the goal
line. Leforce place-kicked the extra
point.


The flrst Western touchdown in
the second period resulted from a
Leforce pass to Fred Provo from
the 48. Provo took the ball on the
East's 20 and outran the defense to
score.


Sacrinity was voted the outstand-
ing player of the game.

Lie OeFOlutlO1 OI 6TltlSn Imperial power
in Southern Asia takes another step with
Ceylon's attainment of full Dominion
status. Henceforth, this big, pear-shaped
island lying off the southern tip of India
will be full-fedged member of the Brit
ish- Commonwealth of Nations ranking
politically with the other Dominions and
enjoying complete independence in the
management of its own affairs.


1t should be noted, however, that Ceylon,
unlike Burma, remains within the Com
monwealth and has concluded agreements
providing for mutual defense and meas
ure of representation by Britain in its
foreign relations. These qualifications
correspond to the realities of the situation.


Ceylon Is relatively small country,
with fewer than 100000 inhabitants,
separated by only narrow strait from
its huge neighbor. India. Ofhand. it
might seem logical for Ceylon to form
part Of an Indian Federation. Yet, despite
its geographical proximity, Ceylons his
toric evolution has been quite distinct
from that of India, giving It's people a
very different psychology and outlook.


The basic dissimilarity Is one of religion.
Buddhism, originally imported from India,
took root and fourished in Ceylon,
whereas 1t died out In India before a
victorious Brahmin reaction And the
difference between Buddhism and Hindu
ism produces profound unlikeness in
culture and ways Of life. Furthermore,
Islam never penetrated Ceylon. Lastly, the
island has been permeated by European
influences for nearly four centuries First
the Portuguese and then the Dutch
formed settlements along the coast, while
the British gained control $50 years ago
and soon subjected the whole island to
their authority. This prolonged European
contact shows, among other matters, in
the existence of native Christian elements
in the coastal regions. Those native
Christians live harmoniously with the
Buddhist majority. However. that is not
the case with a recent immigrant influx
8 During the past half-century great num-
bers of Tamils from Southern India have
come to Ceylon to work on the big planta-
tions. Those Tamils, mostly Hindu in
religion, have kept their identity and are
not on the best of terms with the native
SenegaleSe. That mutual aversion has
tended to strengthen Ceylonese self
consciousness and inhibit any desire for
political union with India. But an inde-
pendent Ceylon would not feel comfortable
beside its mighty neighbor. Hence, part
nership within the British Commonwealth
seems preferable.


For Britain and its other Dominions,
Ceylonese partnership is most welcome,
because Ceylon is vital strategic link in
the chain of communications binding the
British homeland with Australia, New
Zealand and other parts of the Common
wealth in the Far East and the Pacific
Ceylon proved its strategic Importance in
the late war. when it's big naval base of
Trincomalee formed solid bastion
behind which British naval strength
could rally to hold off japanese attacks
across the Bay of Bengal from captured
Malaga and Burma.


1t is thus upon basis of mutual advan-
tage that Ceylon takes its new place in
the British Commonwealth of Nations
That is the best augury that the arrange
ment will prove harmonious and enduring

Justice David A. Pine of District

after lengthy hearing in which the

government.

set up without American approval.

abolishing the force. He praised

against corruption" among German
guards in internee camps.


The American military govern
ment ordered Loritz to do something
about the high number of escapes
this spring, and the 'Kontroll-
dienst," as the special force was
known, then was instituted.

to him for treatment on May %.

clan said she had been treated by
the newest drug for the fever, para
amino benzoic acid, and had re-
sponded well. Miss Stevens case,
the doctor added, was mild.


During 1916 only one case of the

County, but several were reported
in the surrounding area health

CHICAGO, Aug. 29.-The profes-
sional football season, All-America
Conference version, starts tonight
when the Chicago Rockets meet the
Los Angeles Dons before an expected
q, GOO at Soldier Field.


After the inaugural solo, the All
Americas championship race picks
up more speed Sunday when the
Brooklyn Dodgers play at San Fran
cisco and the New York Yankees
visit Buffalo.


The round-robin schedule in which
the eight members of the two-year-
old circuit play seven home games
and seven away continues until mid
December.


The league champion Cleveland
Browns launch their title defense at
home against the Buffalo Bills next
Friday night, and Baltimore, which
replaced Miami in the circuit, gets
underway at home Sunday Septem-
Der 7 against Brooklyn.


The Rocket-Dons clash tonight

the league last year, as coach and
general manager of the Chicago
entry.

cts. operated last year by John L.
Keeshin, Chicago sportsman, will
be watched closely by his own league
and the national loop which has two
strong Chicago Contenders, the
league champion Bears and the
Cardinals.

in a coaching mixup of the season
as Dick Hanley feuded with Kee-
shin and quit, to be followed by a
layer-coaching group and finally
Pat Boland, Hanley's former aid.


Crowley, whose $4,000 per-year
commissionership had four years to
run when he resigned, knows he
has a rugged box-off1ce competition
from the Bears and Cardinals, but
is confident Chicago will support
three professional teams, If they
play good football"

Rocket team which won five, lost

To the Editor of The Star:


The inadequacy of street parking in Wash
ington progressively is growing worse with the
resumption of full scale automobile production.
More parking facilities are required. But until
the city provides these facilities, each driver
should inquire into his parking technique to
determine whether every foot of space is ac-
counted for. Much legal parking is squandered
by thoughtless parking.


Observation will disclose that every city
block in and near the cengested area could
accommodate from one to three more vehicles
without unduly close or illegal parking. Park
ing too close to corners, fireplugs streetear and
bus stops and other automobiles definitely
should not be encouraged, but most. drivers can
judge within five or ten feet the legal distance
from restricted points.


Those individuals who park ten or fifteen
feet farther than the law requires from stop
signs, fireplugs streetcar and bus stops, other
automobiles, ct cetera, are depriving other
drivers of parking space.


ROBERT L. BURCH

MoNTEGO BAY, Jamaica. Sept.
17.-British Colonial Secretary
Arthur Creech Jones left Jamaica
for London yesterday after the
British West Indies conference in
q five-day session had adopted a
resolution accepting the principle
of creating federation of the seven
colonies.


The conference of representatives
of Jamaica, Trinidad, British
Guiana, British Honduras, Barba-
dos and the Leeward and Windward
Islands accepted the principle Of
federation on the Australian model,
with each constituent unit retain
ing control over all matters not
specifically delegated to the federal
government.


The resolution said federation
should not prejudice movements
for self-government in the various
territories. A Caribbean shipping
committee was created to plan the
subsidizing of services linking West
Indies territories and Canada.

commercial negotiations with Bull
garia today and expelled two Bull
garian newspapermen from the coun-

for incidents at Sofia which resulted

for the French press agency.

cial privileges accorded all foreign

drawn from eight other Bulgarian
newspapermen. They will be per-
mtted to continue filing dispatches
to their newspapers, however.


The expelled journalists are Amy
Bakalov, chief of Bulgarian bureau
of information here and correspond
ent for two Sofia weeklies, and
Lovan Strelkov, correspondent for a
Sofia daily newspaper.

that Giorgi Marinov, Bulgarian Min
lister to Paris, had left two days ago
for Sofia, presumably for consulta-
ton after the Greek government had
asked the War Crimes Commission
in London to list Marinov as a war
criminal. The incidents, however,
were not connected.

SARASOTA, Fla, Mar. 26.-As
they swing into the final phase of
their spring training, the Boston Red
Sox, individually and collectively, ap-
pear more firmly convinced than
ever that they can run away with
the American League race again.


Gone with the winter SHOWS are
the hurts and disappointments Joe
Cronin's boys received in the last
World Series, which they entered as
overrated favorites and finished as
a soundly beaten club after Harry
Brecheen of the Cardinals had
dazzled them with his pitching and
Enos Slaughter had mesmerized
them on the base paths.


The Sox, from Ted Williams on
down, realize now that they were
not the all-time wonders they ap-
peared to be in knocking the day
lights out of their own league. At
the same time, however, they have
retained firm appreciation of their
worth, and they are confident they
can win again.


A poll of the teams stars discloses
that they feel they are about 80 per
cent stronger than they were this
time a year ago, mostly because of
greater depth in their pitching. The
Series, they concede, brought out a
numerical weakness in their mound
corps.


Now the Hose apparently have
three additional starters - rockies
who are more or less ready to step
in there and either take their turn
with, or efficiently relieve, the big
men of the staff-Tex Hughson, Bob
Ferriss, Mickey Harris and Joe
Dobson.


The trio, all graduates of the Sox
farm system, are Mel Parnell, left
handler up from Scranton of the
Eastern League; Tommy Fine,
right-hander also from Scranton.
and Harry (Fritz) Dorish, from
Louisville.


All three appear to be finished
products. Fine, after three years in
the service, won % and lost only
three for Scranton last season.
Parnen had 1874 record with the
same club. Dorish, also a three-year
service veteran, posted an 11-4 mark
at Louisville.

FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kans.,
May 5.-The Army continued its in
vestigation today into the Fort
Leavenworth disciplinary barracks
race riot in which one person was
killed and II injured, but made no
comment on its preliminary find
ings.


Normal routine was resumed at
the barracks.


The customary mess hall seating
arrangement, out of which the riot
ing stemmed, was in effect with
Negroes and whites being served in
the same room but at separate
tables.


Long smouldering resentment OF
white prisoners over eating in the
same mess hall with Negroes fared
into the open Friday. The rebellion
was brought under control Satur-
day night.


Col. Graeme Parks, the barracks
commandant, and Brig. Gen. Harry
L. Twaddle headed the investiga-
ton. Gen. Twaddle is on the staff
Of the comanding general of the
5th Army and came here from Chi
cago yesterday.


Attempts were being made to sin
gle out the ringleaders, Col. Parks
said.


Dewey Osborne, 80, white pris-
oner of Mountain City, Tenn, was
beaten to. death in the fighting
among the prisoners. Six other in
mates-four Negroes and two whites
and five guards were injured.


The violence began after three
Negroes attacked a white prisoner
in a shower room.


After hundreds of tear gas bombs
had been lobbed into the cell blocks
containing the rioting men, Col.
Parks issued an unconditional
surrender" ultimatum. .


Two hundred and thirteen Negro
prisoners needed the order first
and six hours later the remaining
514 men involved also surrendered.

MIAMI, Fla, Nov. 2O.-Doctors
credited heroic circus father with
saving the lives of his son and
daughter when they fell from high
wire while performing with the
Ringing Bros. and Barnum g. Bailey
Circus here.


The father, 65-year-old Charles
Alzanas; his son, Harold, 81, and
daughter Hilda, 16, are in Jackson
Memorial Hospital, the two men
badly hurt and the daughter shaken
and bruised.


Charles Alzanas' neck was broken
and his son suffered a fractured
vertebrae, physicians said.
10000 Spectators Watch.
While an estimated 10000 specta-
tors jammed the big top last night
for the shows final appearance in
Miami this season, Harold and Hilda
lost their balance on bicycle atop
the high wire and fell 80 feet to
the ground. They performed with
out net.


The father, watching from the
ring below, saw them topple and
ran beneath them as they fell
Their bodies smashed him to the
ground.


Doctors at the scene said the
fathers action probably saved the
lives of his children.
Bicycle ON Tight Wire.


In the act, Harold Alzanas rode
a bicycle across a 50-foot steel
strand. He held a balance pole in
his hands and Hilda, with no aid
to keep her own balance, sat on his
shoulders. Two other sisters, Elsie
"a, and Minnie, 28, swung from
small trapezes attached to the front
and rear wheels of the bike.


While doctors worked over the
fallen performers, circus working
men rescued the two other sisters
from the high wire.


The act, signed in England last
year, was making its first appear
ance in this country.

SHANGHAI, Oct. 9.-Pro-govern-
ment press dispatches said today
that Chinese Communists have
broken into Yingkow and severe
street fighting Is raging in that
Manchurian port.


The loss of Yingkow would leave
the government only one port in
Manchuria, Hulutao, to the west,
and 1t has little value unless the
Communists are cleared from the
railway to Mukden.


The Communists, striking widely
throughout government-held areas
of Manchuria' against communica-
tion lines and cities, fought into the
suburbs of Yingkow several days
ago.


Reports reaching Peiping said
the Communists broke into Ying-
kow after an artillery lombard
ment. Warplanes supported govern
ment defenders, but the garrison
was depicted as losing ground.


The government announced its
forces had cleared the Tientsin-
Mukden railway from the Great
Wall to Chinhsien, 100 miles to the
Northeast. Hulutao is linked to this
railway by a spur line.


To the north, Communist as
sault in force against Tiehling, 40
miles northeast of Mukden, on the
badly damaged railroad to Chang
chun, was reported under way.

ger-carrying.

then while en- route to Oran reported
motor trouble off Cape Palos, Spain.
1t was not heard from after that.

took off from Algiers and discov-
cred the remains of the craft, the

company yesterday was that the

and remained afloat for a time be-
fore sinking. One report today said

reached the scene during the night,
were sketchy.

The newspaper Ell impartial pub

blood is already running in Man.
aqua streets" and that revolution
was spreading in Nicaragua.


The paper said its story was based
on letters from high Nicaraguan
sources received by Eva Arguello de
Garcia, daughter Of DR.. Leonardo
Arguello, who was ousted as Mic
aragua's president last May.
The story said Gen. Melesio Ben
avides, director of the revolutionary
forces, had smashed national guard
patrols in the Department tot Chon-
tales, killing lieutenant and IA
men. It added that the revolution
airy movement was growing daily
and that countrywide commercial
strike was being organized.


Reports of revolution in Nicaragua
circulated widely last month. Gen.
Anastasio Somoza, former presi-
dent and now chief of the Nicara-
guam national guard, announced
September 9 that the country was
calm after raiders made surprise
attack on an army garrison at La
India mine the night before.
September 20, Gen. Somoza an
nounced that the revolutionary
movement had been crushed.

Eighteen overseas plane flights
normally terminating in New York
were diverted to National Airport
yesterday and today. creating an
unprecedented jam for customs and
immigration officials.


More than 500 persons bound for
New York. among them several
Greek, italian and French war
brides, landed at the airport during
the SO hours following shutdown of
La Guardia Field because Of snow
conditions.


Government officials and airline
personnel were taxed to the limit
to receive and care for the pas
sengers, most of whom did not
speak English.


Six of the flights, including one
originating in Cairo and carrying
the war brides, were Trans World
Airlines.


There were 10 Greek war brides,
all of whom had expected to be
greeted by their fiances in New
York. Instead, they tried to make
their wishes known to Government
and airline agents.


Physicians and customs officials
worked through yesterday and last
night without rest. examining the
passengers and checking their bag
gage. They were turned over to
others who sought hotel rooms fpr.

CAIRO, Oct. 23-The battle
against Egypt's cholera epidemic has
become an outstanding example of
international cooperation.


The United States, Britain, Soviet
Russia, France, italy, Holland,
Switzerland, Lebanon, Syria and
1raq have made vaccine, blood
plasma or drugs available to the
Egyptian government. Offers of
supplies from Brazil, Sweden, Po-
land, South Africa and China have
been accepted.


Nations everywhere are watching
Egypts campaign against the cpl
demic which, in it's first 81 days, re-
suited in 2,6O6 cases and 568 deaths.


Disease Could Spread.


Medical circles emphasize that the
disease, thriving on poverty and un-
sanitary conditions, would spread
quickly in the Middle East If con-
certed and drastic measures were
not taken. Some Middle Fasteners
feel that, if cholera swept unchecked
through this part Of the world, the
stability of the existing regimes
would be shaken and the field made
more fertile for Communist agita-
ton. Prime Minister Nokrashi
Pasha said that only prompt out
side help in anti-cholera supplies
averted a catastrophe in Egypt.


Cholera, with its high death rate,
was once common in parts of the
Middle East. In Iraq, big epidemics
used to occur about every four years,
but the last one, when some 1000
cases were reported, was in 1881.
It was in Egypt that Robert Koch,
the German bacteriologist, con-
Quoted much of his research that
ended in his isolating the cholera
germ in 1883.


European epidemics between 1880
and 1895 reached the United States.


The governments of Palestine,
Syria, the Lebanon, Iraq, Iran and
Turkey are taking the strictest
measures to prevent an outbreak of
cholera in their territories.


Air Traffic Suspended.


Air traffic between Iran and Egypt
has been suspended. Similar pre-
cautions have been taken by various
European governments, particularly
Greece, Italy and Spain.


Units of the United States feet
cancelled proposed visit to Alex
andria and the Arab League Coun-
Gil met in Beirut instead of Cairo.


Egyptian troops have isolated af-
fected areas, and aircraft have been
employed for disinfection purposes,
including DDT spraying. Special de-
contamination squads have bee,
created, and the government has
banned the import into Cairo Of
produce from the infected areas

was postponed indefinitely and all

Washington launched it's game
with Boston in light rain yester-
day and finished in man-made fog
created by Denny Galehouse, 35-
year-old fugitive from the st. Louis

Galehouse, who beat Detroit June

season.

eight innings with 40 deficit,
turning the relief chores over to
Chick Pieretti, who was no sensa-
ton, yielding four more runs.


Sid's wildness cost the Mats two
runs in the first inning. After Buddy
Lewis had leaped against the right
field fence to stab Wally Moses
drive, Hudson walked Johnny Pesky
and Ted Williams. Sam Mele
forced Williams, but Sid loaded the
bases by walking Bobby Doerr and
in that predicament Leon Culherson
singled to right, scoring Pesky and
Mele.


When Lewis throw to the plate
darted past Al Evans, Doerr con-
tinued to third and Culberson
streaked to second but Hudson
averted additional damage by get
ting Murrell Jones on a pop fly.


That situation existed until the
fifth, when Pesky's triple to left
center and Williams single to center
fashioned another Boston run. The
Red Sox boosted the score to 40
in the seventh when Williams blasted
triple to the left field corner and
scored after Mele flied to Lewis.


Mats Hopes Dissipate.


Whatever hopes the Mats were
harboring of producing rally dis
sipated with Pieretti's appearance in
the ninth. With one out he pitched
a single to Pesky. then walked Will
liams and Mele to load the bases.


Doerr punched single to center,
nearly removing Pieretti's head in
the process and scoring Pesky and
williams. When Eddie Pellagrini
singled to right, scoring Mele, Man.
ager Ossie Bluege waved Milo Cam
dini to the mound.


Candini disposed Of Jones on. a
fly to Joe Grace, but the fourth Bos-
ton run of the inning was sprayed
across the plate when Roy Partee
singled to left, scoring Doerr from
second. Eddie Yost brought mer-
ciful halt to the outburst by throw
ing out Galehouse.


Washington first hit was de-
livered by Yost leading off in the
first inning when he singled to left.
The Mats second hit also was the
work of Yost. who doubled to left
center with two out in the third
and proceeded no further because
Lewis flied to Mele.


Priddy Hits Into Double-Play.


Washington next faint hope
ffickered in the fourth when Mickey
Vernon and Stan Spence walked
successfully with none out, but
Grace flied to Mele and feeblehit-
ting Jerry Priddy drilled into
double-play.


The Mats didn't get another man
ON base until the seventh, when
Priddy singled off Pesky's glove with
two out and Evans singled to right,
sending Priddy to third. Cecil
Travis then batted for Mark Christ
man and lifted fly to Williams.


Washington didn't disturb Gale
house in the eighth or ninth. He
set the Mats down in order to snatch
his third win of the year.

DEAL, England, Mar. 8.-The Ira,
70o0-ton Greek coal ship built in
the United States, exploded and
broke in two today after running
aground on English Channel sands,
but her 34-man crew was rescued
despite panic in which some were
injured.


The Ira. formerly the American
Liberty ship Harry Percy, was
carrying coal from Newport News,
Va, to Antwerp on her first Atlantic
crossing under the Greek flag when
she went aground on the treacherous
Goodwin Sands about midnight.
She shattered herself five hours
later.


Seamen from Walmer took the
crew off in lifeboats. Jim Rich of
Walmer, directing the rescue aboard
the Ira, said he and shipmates were
swept away by mad rush of Greek
seamen for the lifeboats. Coxswain
Fred Upton, who was in a lifeboat
300 yards from the Greek ship when
she fell apart, said he had never
seen such panic in all my life"


None of the rescued was reported
injured severely.

The decision involved labor dis
putes affecting plant guards of Jones
& Laughlin Steel Corps Otis

& Co., Indianapolis maker of tools
and arnor plate.


Jones g. Laughlin contended

definition of that term as ANY per-
son acting in the interest of an
employer, directly or indirectly"


Two Separate Decisions.


The high court handed down two
separate decisions.


In the Jones & Laughlin case
the courts 5-4 opinion was written
by Justice Murphy. Chief Justice
vinson and Justices Frankfurter
jackson and Burton dissented.


In the Atkins case. the majority
opinion was written by Justice
Murphy, with dissents noted by the
Chief Justice and Justices Frank
furter and Jackson.


Lower Court Overruled.


The decisions overturned lower
court rulings.


The United States Circuit Court
in Cincinnati decided the Jones and
Laughlm guards were employees, but
said it was improper for the Ma
tional Labor Relations Board to per-
nit their organization by the same
union which represented produc-
ton employees. The Circuit Court
stated that under Ohio law, the
guards were municipal police whose
obligations to the public were in
compatible with obligations to the
union-the CLIO United Steelworkers
Of America.


In the Atkins case, the Circuit
Court in Chicago said plant guards
were not employees under terms OF
the labor act. The Atkins guards
were deputy policemen of the city
of Indianapolis.


During the war guards of both
plants we're members of the civil
ian auxiliary to military police
under arrangements set up by the
War Department.

battle, which centered in the down.

sticks and threw bricks.

iery of the Assembly chamber where

ing them.

Down with Yankee imperialism"
and many of them jeered cabinet
ministers arriving at the Assembly
building.

Rodeo clowns do lot more

TASBo FULKERsoN has been rodeo clown
for the past l8 years. In between the
calf-roping, bronco-busting and bulldogging
events, Jasbo - in checked shirt and trou-
sers miles too big for him - BUNDLES about
the arena in highly humorous fashion
Rodeo fans think he's one of the funniest
men around.


In his l8 years on the circuit, Jasbo has
also had his arm broken seven times, his
legs more times than he can remember and
has been gored more times than he likes to
think of. He and his buddies have also won
the respect of several hundred cowboys
whose lives they've saved.


Take the Fort Worth rodeo in March,
1916. A Brahma bull had just thrown its
rider. Paving the ground nervously, the
animal suddenly wheeled, lowered its head
and charged the dazed contestant.


Spectators held their breath. No one
noticed clown loping across the turf, wav-
ing a battered derby hat No one, that is,
except the bull, who caught the hat
flush across the snout.


The brute veered off its course, halted
and turned to glare at the clown. The clown
glared back. Then he waggled his fingers in
a highly derogatory manner. The crowd
loved it, roared with laughter.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 20-Visions of
Is white Christmas and a more

Chinese they portend starvation

Events of this pre- Christmas week

Shanghai had its first snowfall of

mometer went down only to 81, but
the frigidity was enough to exact
heavy toll Of lives. BY early yes
terday 10 corpses-60 OF them chill

That figure was only half the
number of bodies found after last
years first cold spell, but the wealth.
er man-who promises white
Christmas - forecasts even colder
weather.


Fish Profits Enormous.
AS If nature itself were not cruel

operators plan to wax rich against
| UNRRA efforts to increase catches
and lower prices.


New Year Day will be the signal
for the big squeeze play.
This cruel plot began when, at
the urgent request of the Chinese
movement, UNRRA sent out l26
modern fishing boats to help haul
in needed supplies of sea food. The
Shanghai fish market, which has
fattened off the fish scarcity, was
Mortified. To head off the UNRRA
fleet, the market operators promptly
put forward a fish-catch quota
calling for only five UNRRA vessels.

calculations. In light of the alb

quite unacceptable"
All the UNRRA fishing boats,
happily, are in operation-now.

Reminding them that Shanghai

Students at Futan University,

udiced and unfair" stories about the
current student disorders. Two re-

A heavy rain washed out student

text:
In tightening safety rules for
nonscheduled air carriers. the Civil
Aeronautics Board has taken such
an obviously sensible step that one
wonders why 1t was not taken
earlier.


The nonscheduled carriers are
passenger or cargo planes that are
let out for hire but have no certifi-
Gates for scheduled routes. They
are not part of the regular airlines,
and up to now they have been less
regulated. With the new rules, how
ever, they will have to meet require
ments almost as strict, and in some
cases Identical, as regards pilot
flight time limitations, aircraft
maintenance, landing procedure, etc.


Accident statistics emphasize the
timeliness of putting these tighter
regulations into effect. Thus last
year, according to the CAB, the non
scheduled carriers suffered seven
fatal crashes in which 16 crew men,
bers and SO passengers were killed.
AS estimated by Senator Brewster,
chairman of the Senate Subcommit-
tee on Aviation, these figures-in
proportion to the number of passen-
ger miles flown-represent cas-
ualty rate nearly eight times that of
the scheduled lines, which last year
had nine crashes, killing % crew
members and rs passengers. These
two sets of tragic statistics have
been read without differentiation by
the public and undoubtedly have
contributed to the fairly widespread
impression that regular air travel
has been growing more dangerous
when actually, as shown by the
statistics, it has been growing safer.


The newly extended rules consti-
tute a sound corrective measure cal
'culated to save lives. Given more Of
the same promptly, wherever needed
in either the scheduled or nom
scheduled field, and the safety rec
ord of American aviation will al
most certainly continue to improve.
headline: For Greater Air Safety

STOCKHOLM, Feb. 17.-Barbara
Ann Scott, young Canadian beauty,
has added the women's world figure
skating championship to her fast
growing collection of triumphs.


The 1S-year-old blonde from Ot-
tawa won the world crown yesterday
following sensational display of
free skating which entranced the
crowd who poured out on the ice to
offer her congratulations after she
was declared the winner.


Eight of the nine judges placed
Miss Scott first and awarded her two
sixes-the highest possible score
after her dazzling performance.


Trailing Miss Scott, who posted
24S.37 points for both the school
and free skating, was Daphne
Walker Of England and Gretchen
Merrill of Boston. Miss Walker had
334.09 and Miss Merrill 327.76 points.


Miss Scott, Canadian and North
American champion, earlier in the
year had won the European figure
skating championship at Davos
Platz, Switzerland, during which she
also was graded at six, the first time
any one ever was graded six at
Davos Platz.


In Yesterdays competition, Miss
Merrill, who had a slim lead over
Miss Walker after the first day, fell
during the middle of her dancing
exhibition and lost whatever chance
she had of winning.


Miss Eileen Seigh of Brooklyn,
who was 10th following the school
skating Saturday, wound up fourth
after a sensational performance in
the free skating yesterday.


Although Miss Scott won't be
home until March or later, plans
already were being made in Ottawa
for civic reception.


Messages of congratulations went
out to the young star, headed by one
from Prime Minister Mackenzie
King. The Prime Minister said Cam
ada was delighted with your we'll
merited victory" Governor Cen
eral Viscount Alexander cabled, I'VE

congratulations"

history Of the Santa Anita Handicap.


Interest now turns toward the run.
ming Of the 100000 Santa Anita
Derby next Saturday, with q fine
array Of 3-year-olds battling for the
rich purse, but racing circles con-
tinue to rehash the downfall of the
Calumet Stables long tailed cham.
pion in the big race Saturday.


The handicap king ran fifth In
the mile-and-a-quarter classic, two
and q half lengths back of a chal-
lenger from Chile, Olhaverry.


Stitch Again, one time $500
claiming horse, ran second, and two
California bred candidates, Pere
Time and See-Tee-See, grabbed of
third and fourth places. leaving
Armed, the even-money choice, to
run In the also-ran class.


May Have Been Tired.


Jockey Doug Dobson, who rode
Armed to victory in two previous
stake engagements In Florida and
flew here last Tuesday with the
handsome gelding determined to
make it three in row on successive
week ends, said after the race they
couldn't find room to move ahead
In the stretch.


To veteran experts, however. It
appeared that Armed simply tired
In the final stages and couldn't COLI
lar the leader at this point. Stitch
Again, or hold of the rushes Of
Olhaverry, Pere Time and See-Tee-
See.


Others said Armed may have
been tired from too much racing,
that the airplane trip here cost him
strength. Still others said the blis-
tering mile, raced in 1855, with
the speedy Artillery setting the early
pace, was too much for the favorite,
who carried top weight Of 129
pounds. Artillery, for instance,
packed 110; Alhaverry, an '8-year.
old gray. horse, had 116; Stitch
Again, 112, and Pere Tine, 108.


In any event, Armed made his
move at the far turn, drove UP to
second entering the stretch. and
then hung.


Racing People Astounded.


The finish marked another de-
feat for name horses. Equipoise and
Twenty Grand were shut out by
Azucar In the first running Of the
race In 1895, but in fairness 1t must
be remembered that both great
thoroughbreds were past their peak
at the time. The next year Dis
covery ran seventh to Top Row,
and in 1898 a favored Seabiscuit
lost by head to the colt Stage
hand, who carried 80 pounds less
than the Biscuit.


But Armed supposedly Is at the
peak of his career. That Is why
veteran racing people frankly said
they were "astounded."


The most disappointed was his
owner, Warren Wright. who flew
here from Miami last week. He
wanted that victory to send the
gelqing into second place in ths

week end.


Shoppers also found butter up a
cent or two over early week prices

meatless day plan and general con-
sumner resistance to higher prices as
among, the reasons for cheaper
pork, others saw it mostly as sea-
sonal decline.


Hog Run" in Full Swing.


The annual hog run" on the
slaughter houses began about three
weeks ago. The replacement cost
of pork in the West declined to
6 cents the past week, making
total of IL to 13 cents a pound the
last two weeks.


Then, too, the unseasonal warm
weather throughout the country
has discouraged much pork eating
and helped build up supplies.


Whether the lower prices con-
tinue for any period depends strict
ly on supply versus demand, with
the possibility that cold weather
in the production areas might help
shove the prices up, it was said.


Although no declines in beef,
lamb or poultry appeared imminent,
some merchandisers thought reduc-
tions possible if enough consumers
turn to pork for heavy buying.

mining in this country the hazards
of the miners trade were far greater
than they are today. Dust explo-

"black damp" were fairly common.
The fatality rate was correspond
ingly high.


Since the establishment in 1910
of the United States Bureau of
Mines, however, the number of
accidents has been reduced remark
ably and the annual toll in lives
has been growing smaller and
smaller. About the time of the
bureaus birth, for example, approx
imately five lives were lost for every
million tons of coal mined. BY 1920
the deaths had dropped nearly 5
per cent and by 1925 the decrease
amounted to IL per cent. The safety
record has continued to improve in
recent years.


Coal dust and gas explosions of
the type which apparently caused
the Centralia disaster have been the
subject of intensive study by the
Bureau of Mines. As a result of
these studies, many of them con-
Quoted in the bureaus own labora-

of combating these explosions have
been worked out and put into gen.

against dust dangers are dust-tight
cars, special dust barriers, constant
removal of dust accumulations and
wetting down of tunnels. Gas is

gas or dust blasts are forbidden.

ATHENS, Sept. 1l.-Liberal Pre-
mier Themistokles Sophoulis and
his new cabinet won an almost
unanimous vote of confidence from
the Greek Parliament yesterday.


The vote was 279 for the govern
ment and two against.


Just before adjournment, Par
lament was presented a draft bill
of the terms of an unconditional
general amnesty for Greek guer-
rilla fighters.


Under the terms Of the bill, guer-
rillas who surrender will be freed
Immediately after registering with
the public prosecutor of the district
in which they give themselves up
The draft limits the amnesty period
to one month, but this may be
increased by royal decree.

no official statement came from

homes in smyth County and poured
into the streets Of Marion yesterday
while high winds again lashed Lee
County, where q windstorm late
Sunday demolished houses, uprooted
trees and damaged crops.


Heavy rains plowed down the side
OF Staleys Knob, south of Marion,
sending Staleys Greek over its bank,
flooding homes and drowning hogs
and chickens along the stream
Twenty business places were flooded
as the creek surged into Marion's
main street. Fruit stands were
washed away and melons and fruit
floated down the stream into the
Holston River. At the same time
fish from q nearby hatchery were
swimming in Marion's streets.


No loss of life was reported from
any part of the county.


High winds In Lee County caused
little damage compared with the
havoc left by Sundays twister along
a patch 10 miles long and from
200 to $50 yards wide. Striking 6
miles west of Ewing the Sunday
storm uprooted more than a hum
dred trees, demolished at least three
houses and several barns, tore roofs
from other buildings, killed some
livestock and damaged corn and
tobacco crops before 1t played out
beyond Rose Hill.


There were unconfirmed reports
that a child was killed when q tree
was blown against a mountain cabin
in an isolated section of the county
but those reports could not be veri-
fed.

JERUSALEM, Feb. 5.-More
than $50 British civilians left
Palestine under the British
Army's Operation Polly today,
taking off from Aqir airdrome in
Royal Air Force Halifax planes
bound for Egypt.


A later dispatch from Cairo said
the planes engaged in evacuating
British civilians from Palestine
landed there shortly before noon
and that the occupants were taken
to British homes in the suburbs.


The shuttle flight system was ex-
pected to remove at least 500 British
women and children from the Holy
Land trouble spot by nightfall.


More than 1000 others are await
ing their turn in Sarafand or Haifa
holding centers, where the army has
turned military cantonments into
dispersal points for civilians being
evacuated to lessen the govern
ments security commitments in
violence-threatened Palestine.
Meanwhile, the cities the civilians
left were teeming with a reshuffle
of the populace designed to put all
government officials and other re-
naming civilians of British nation
ality under heavy guard.


Nearly 1000 Jews have been dis
possessed in Jerusalem to make way
for security compounds and many
hotels and boarding houses are un-
der orders to accept no guests unless
certified by the Palestine govern
ment. Spot identity checks are con-
tinuing, with foot patrols of COM
bined police and military personnel
touring the city.


All roads to Jerusalem still are
blocked by armored patrols.
High Commissioner Gen. Sir Alan
Cunningham was one of those pres
ent at Aqir Airfield when the first
planes left. The field itself was
under heavy guard.


There still was no official word as
to when, or If, Dow Bella Gruner.
condemned member of Irgun Zvai
Leumi, would hang, but the respite
granted him last week apparently
still was in effect. Most sources be-
lieve that the execution of Gruner
will touch off new and terrible vio-
llence.

nude, mutilated body of Mrs. Doro-

day under pepper tree in vacant
lot near her home. Police said she
had been raped and strangled.
The woman left home last night
to meet her 15-year-old daughter,
Maycille, at a playground on Slausen

appointment and did not return
home last night.


Mrs. Montgomery's clothes had

head was crushed. Her blood
stained automobile was found near
the playground today by Maycille
and another daughter, Mrs. Roselle
Jones, 18.


The woman's husband, Thomas F.
Montgomery, As, reported her miss
ing last night.


James Kennedy, who lives near
the playground, told authorities he
saw a middle-aged man step from
the Montgomery automobile about
1880 O'Clock last night and walk
away.


Officers believe Mrs. Montgomery,
an attractive woman, was accosted
as she waited near the playground
for her daughter, forced into an
other automobile, driven to the va
cant lot and attacked and slain.


The method of the murder was
similar in some respects to that of
Elizabeth Short, %, known as the
BLACK Dahlia," whose nude, mu-
tilated body was found in vacant
lot January Is.


This was the fourth sex murder
here this year. The killers of Jeanne
AFFORD French and Evelyn Winters
have not been apprehended.
