CygnuS, the Swan, Is Scudding across
the sky these December nights. Bare and
sere are the level meadows and sidehill
pastures. The swamp lies open and naked
where few months ago all was dim and
concealed. Muted is the music of brooks
and creeks and the waters move slowly
downward to the sea. Fences and walls
are brown-gray stitching on the landscape
and the trees on the hardwood ridges are
starkly silhouetted against the sky.


Windrows of sodden leaves are packed
against the sides of barns and corn cribs
Black pennants of smoke idle upward from
farmhouse chimneys and drift slowly
away-hyphens on Decembers gray pages
The hollow ringing of axe blows echoes
from the woodlot above the orchard and
the long, thin, lonesome whistle of the
train travels far over the countryside in
the still air. Gone now is the shrill rant
ing of the blue jays. The winter staying
birds come around the farmstead A few
lonesome crows walk slowly among the
tepees Of corn stalks.


Gray is the last month of the year. The
stratus and nimbus clouds hang low over
fields and hills. Earth is patiently waiting
for snow to cover her hard breast. He who
is sensitive can almost feel the mood of
expectancy. Short are the hours of day
light and sudden the dropping of dark
ness. Stand on hillside on quiet
last month day and wait for the first
flakes to come. wandering down through
the air. At first there are only few,
meandering irregularly to their resting
place. Minute by minute the numbers
increase. Hills across the valley are shut
from view The storm closes In. Nature
is closing her book4

August creeps over the land on muff1ed.
sticky feet. Sirius, the Dog Star ascends
his throne for period of regal uncomfort-
ableness. brassy sun courses across a
washed-blue sky and at night moist sultri-
ness lies like heavy blanket on the Earth.
This is the other quiet month OF the cycle.
Twice each year before the beginning of
new seasons, in February and in March,
the countryside is peculiarly silent.


Through hot days and heavy nights the
corn pushes toward maturity. Go to the
edge OF field in the light of the Thunder
Moon and you can hear the corn ladies
rustic their bustles. Shorn fields and
meadows browse through sitting days.
Cows spend the noon hours beneath pro-
tecting trees and the hens gather in the
shade OF the tangled blackberries. Grass
hoppers make noises like fishermen wind
ing their reels; bees and insects explore
the flowers in the perennial border beneath
farm kitchen windows.


The first goldenrods lift yellow plumes
along weathered rail fences; hardhack
holds its purple spires against rocky up
land pastures. Scraggly-armed sumacs
hold high their wine-red pennants and ad :
vance-scout autumn asters reflect the blue
OF the sky. Through the quiet days the
wildlife of field and wood slips about its
business. Sometimes huge black thunder
heads below up from the horizon and
Vulcan hurls his forked javelins of light
ming. Dusk comes on reluctantly and sun.
set glory fingers above the horizon
Crickets play their monotone fiddles and
the firefiies stage their green-gold lantern
ballet over lawn and garden. "A whippoor
will sounds his poignant, plaintive call
from the wall behind the barn. Taps to an
August day.

MOSCOW. Dec. 17.-Izvestia pub
lished dispatches from many parts
of the Soviet Union today reporting
that since rationing was abolished
Sunday, there has been wide scale
consumer buying in a "holiday-like'
atmosphere.


Russian citizens currently are
trading their old rubles for new at
rates varying up to 10 to /. The
currency revaluation and the end
Of rationing were announced in the
same edict.


Izvestia said 10000 retail stores
had been repaired or organized anew
in a short period, and were selling
goods.


"The stores have large quantities
of goods" the newspaper said.


The article cited the trade minis
tries of Armenia, Moldavia and
Uzbekistan. however, as Tagging
behind" in the development OF
trade.


Farmer Markets Urged.


"The network of stores in Chelya-
binsk, Rostov and Kirov regions is
not sufficiently organized" the
article said. Many stores remain
unoccupied and the law giving
ground floors in certain new build
ings to stores has not been carried
out everywhere. It is now up to the
workers that all mass goods should
reach the consumers and rapidly.
Collective stores and cooperative
stores should be organized more
energetically and more farmer
markets should be set up"


The article said collective farms
were selling more produce to the
state and that a huge amount of
business had been done Throughout
the Soviet Union on Monday. Many
stories were said to have doubled
their staffs. -


The gaStronomeS-Moscow's super
delicatessens-also are selling un-
rationed food now. Foreigners who
formerly had their own gastronome
to sell them their rationed food now
have been told by Russian author
tiles they must purchase on the same
bases as all Soviet citizens, through
regular retail channels. This also
affects diplomats.


THE consumer is boss" Izvestia
said.


Moscow Has 800 New Stores.


The newspaper said 800 new stores
and $50 kiosks had been opened in
Moscow and that more than 1000
stores now were selling bread in the
capital. Similar conditions were
said to prevail in Leningrad.


A dispatch from Kiev, capital of
the Ukraine, said 400 new stores
were opened there and that sales

new stores and kiosks were opened.


Izvestia said hardly any bread
queues existed.


A Tashkent dispatch said buy
ing was in progress without inter-
ruption. A Kharkov dispatch said
serious deficiencies" had developed
in the preparation of stores for
business and that in one district
there was not enough food.

by the black market for American
cigarettes.

I19.-The buildings and supplies

The annual report Of the Washington
Criminal Justice Association, while show
ing that the climbing crime rate here In
1946 was in line with country wide trends,
is anything but reassuring. 1t is true that
all large cities have experienced post
war increase in serious crimes. But some
of the data in the associations report
bear out previous assertions that the
crime rate could be lowered here by more
effective law enforcement.


For example, the association for several
years has supported the pleas of the
Police Department and the Commissioners
for legislation authorizing additional
patrolmen and facilities with which to
reorganize the precinct system. The need
for new police precinct in the Benning
area has been particularly urged, on the
ground that lawlessness was certain to
increase there because of ineffective
supervision from Anacostias Eleventh
Precinct Station-far across the Anacostia
River. The report now reveals that the
fears of police and citizens have material
lied. For it was in the Eleventh Precinct
that the greatest rise in juvenile crime
was recorded last year. This rise occurred
despite the fact that the overall increase
in juvenile crime for Washington in 1916
was negligible.


The association points out that steps
finally are being taken to detach the
Benning area from Anacostia precinct and
to give that congested but badly neglected
section the type of police protection 1t
deserves. That reform has been made
possible by appropriations for construc-
ton of a precinct station in Benning But
there must be sufficient policemen to
patrol this area and other troublesome
spots more thoroughly. The association
declares that Washington needs con-
siderably larger force to fight postwar
crime. The distressingly large number
of unsolved cases cited in its report bears
out this contention

Washington settled down to It's
normal routine today after a Memo
rial Day week end which was fea-
tured by almost perfect weather and
a record transportation flow since
before the war.
Union Station officials said that
home-returning holiday crowds yes
terday afternoon and evening were
the largest since the war. A steady
flow of travellers kept returning in
the early hours of the morning to-
day.


Likewise National Airport officials
said the traffic jam there yesterday
was far greater than expected"


Planes Can't Handle Load.


Despite last weeks plane crashes
incoming and outgoing planes were
packed, officials said. Long lines of
persons waited throughout the day
in hopes of getting reservations
through last-minute cancellations.


Capital and American Airlines
added extra planes between here
and New York, Pittsburgh and Nor
folk.
Railroads reported many standees
among the passengers, SO great was
the crush. Buses also did big busi-
ness, especially those carrying back
passengers from Maryland and Vir-
ginia resorts.


Trains Run Extra Sessions.


The Pennsylvania and Baltimore
and Ohio Railroads operated extra
sections on their trains to meet the
travel demand. Some of the packed
aisles reminded railroad officials of
wartime travel conditions.


The fine holiday weather here
made Washington a perfect play
ground for the thousands of out-of-
town visitors here as well as the
home folks.


Swimming pools and parks were
filed with visitors and the Potomac
was the scene of many sailing par
ties. Highways in nearby Maryland
and Virginia were crowded with
Sunday motorists.

and Lamoine, slept through the
tragedy. He was in an auto trailer,
about 100 yards away, and was not
awakened until the arrival of the
fire engine.

LONDON, Feb. 6 LR.-British
leaders summoned Jewish Agency
representatives into an unscheduled
conference today apparently to dis
close details of a cabinet plan on
Palestine.


The cabinet discussed the Holy
Land this morning for the third
successive day, before Foreign Sec
retary Bevin called the Jewish lead
ers together.


Informed Whitehall sources gave
this picture:


There were two distinct plans
when British ministers tackled the
subject Tuesday. One was Colonial
Secretary Arthur Creech Jones
formula for partitioning the coun-
try into independent Jewish and
Arab states Immediately. The Sec
ond was Mr.. Bevin's scheme to
modify the so-called Morrison plan
for creating semi-autonomous Arab
and Jewish provinces in the Holy
Land.


A compromise settlement was
reached in principle but details
were still being hammered out.


Mr.. Creech Jones changed his
partition Immediately" proposal to
partition within five years." He
also called on the cabinet not to
impose any ceiling on immigration
into the Jewish zone, and to abolish
the Palestine police force.


Mr.. Bevin disagreed with Mr.
Creech Jones suggestions. The
foreign secretary, supported by
Prime Minister Attlee and Defense
Minister A. v. Alexander, demanded
a maximum Jewish immigration fig
ure. He urged that If the Jewish
Agency rejected his settlement Brit
ain should hand over the mandate
to the United Nations.

meeting last night unanimously op-

then adopted a resolution directing
its 14-man executive to draft a full
answer to the British Gin accord
with the sentiments" of the

May Withdraw Recognition.

recognition from the agency.

night said there was mot the

NEW DELHI, June 14.-Mohandas
K. Gandhi, speaking from. cross
legged position on the dias. told the
AIl-India Congress Committee of
400 today 1t should accept the Brit
ish plan for partition of India even
though he himself has opposed par
|tition


/ The committee recessed tonight
without a vote But approval Of the
plan was considered virtually cer-
tain after the limited but vociferous
opposition has had its say. Four
teen speakers opposed partition to-
day during six hours of debate in
the steaming hall which once was
an American Army barracks.


Session Open to Press.


Unlike the Moslem League action
in approving partition last week.
which was In secret meeting, the
session was open to the press, such
members of the public as could jam
into the hall and all who wished to
listen over loudspeaker system on
the outside.


Gandhi argued that the Congress
Party leaders had committed them
selves to partition, and the delegates
should support their stand because
they are after all your representa-
tives."


A resolution by the forward block,
once headed by Subhas Chandra
Bose who led the Indian National
Army which fought alongside the
japanese in Burma, denounced the
Mountbatten plan as "treacherous
design to viyisect India.


States Face Challenge.


Party leaders made ready res
olution to challenge the right of the
princely states to declare their in
dependence from the rest of India
when the British leave the country.


The rulers of two states, Hydera-
bad and Travanacore, already have
announced they will become inde-
pendent. One Is predominantly
Hindu and the other predominantly
Moslem.


In addition newspapers printed
reports that half dozen Sikh hill
states in Punjab planned shortly to
declare their independence.

Changchun-b bound reinforcements.

ceeded in cutting the Manchurian
railway at several points between
Kungchuling and Changchun.

government to make every effort to

leaders.

If the talks are revived, they would
be foredoomed to failure. There is
only one way OF achieving unifica-

skirmishes in Shansi Province of
China proper, but Tong said heavy
battles were expected soon.

fendant Gen. Sadao Araki with the
secret Manchurian diary" Of
Japan's Kwantung army for 1888.


japanese witnesses have told the

minister congratulating Manchukuo
officials for cooperation" with the

Jehol Province. The telegram was
part of the Manchurian diary which
supposedly contains all official or
ders between Tokyo authorities and
military forces in the field.


Araki readily admitted author
ship of the telegram, but appeared
surprised at production Of the diary.

leaders on trial.

holiday week end at beaches and

The District, over Sunday, was
free of fatal accidents, but Mary
land already has counted six dead
and Virginia four from traffic and
other accidents.


Picnics, boating, outdoor sports
and just plain loafing featured the
day for those who chose to avoid
the Labor Day rush and spend a
quiet holiday at home. The down.
town streets were almost deserted
as practically all business was sus-
pended.


Although hotels were filled with
visitors crowding the traditional
Labor Day vacation deadline, the
city was 6lieter than on the aver
age Sunday. The city's spots of
interest were being visited on about
the same scale as the usual week
end.


Transportation facilities, released
from the strain of the Friday
night and Saturday getaway rush,
were running normally today, But
the railroads, airlines and buslines
were lining up extra sections for an
other outburst tonight.


One of the Districts few rains
during August, AZ of an inch falling
for an hour last night, brought re-
lief from heat reaching 81 degrees at
4:10 pm. yesterday. Despite the
shower, August's rainfall measured
only 1.81 inches and was 2.20 inches
below normal for the month.

to help keep the temperature down
to 88 degrees today. Widely scat
tered showers expected in Virginia
were expected to miss the District.

night, the Weather Bureau said. :.


A low pressure area moving in
from the Midwest may shoot the
temperature up to 80 degrees tomor-
row. But in its wake the Weather
Bureau sees a better measure OF
rain than has fallen recently, reach

Wednesday, and cooling things con-
siderably.


The churches yesterday took cog
nizance of the holiday to emphasize
the need for better labor relations.

cabinet had decided the partition oi

question.

cabinet had discussed both the
unilateral imposition of partition

informant said, while Foreign Sec

PARRY SOUND, Ontario, Aug.
IA Georgian Bay pilot, flying at
400 feet, six miles from the main
land here yesterday, spotted the
frantic waving of a sweatshirt and
brought rescue to two Columbus,
Ohio, girls, lost more than 20 hours.


The two girls were Mary Vorys
13-year- -old daughter of Represent
ative Vorys of Ohio, and her a.
year-old cousin, Elinor Vorys. With
a light outboard craft, they had set
out Wednesday evening. The Vorys
live at 27O2 Wisconsin avenue when
in Washington.


Minutes after a storm broke, they
found themselves on a barren, 30
foot square rock. Their 14-foot craft
was smashed and the motor broken


The rescue was completed when a
boat owned by John David Eaton
Toronto department store owner
skinned through the open water
and picked up the half-famished
girls, shivering in the cool night air,
their clothing soaked.


The plane pilot, AL Dinnan, said
the girls had travelled miles from
their starting point. The storm
swelled just after sunset and they
reached the rock before dark. Their
battered boat was hurled and tossed
like a cork. Waves finally tore the
craft away from the rock, and it was
recovered some distance from where
the girls were located.

The young writer. whose first
novel, Boston Adventure" won crit
ical acclaim, publishes a second
which is likely to add considerably
to herr literary reputation. "The
Mountain Lion" is an extraordinarily
sensitive study of childhood.


Miss Stafford's new novel is, in
fact, more than that implies. It is
more than the story of the two
children who are its central figures,
their struggles, fears, hopes and de-
spairs. The grown people who are
close to these baff1ed, thwarted
children emerge, largely through
their eyes, clear and fully proper
toned, not the great shadowy crea-
lures that most books about children
make them out.


Ralph is 10, his sister Molly 8
when the story opens They live in a
spacious place on an edge of Los
Angeles in the days before Holly
wood became an industry and SYM
Dol. They lived with their shallow,
pretentious mother, a widow, and
their more glamorous older sisters,
Leah and Rachel. The intimate cir
Gle includes the minister, vain and
intolerant, and his scrawny wife.
Nature and scarlet fever have cursed
Ralph and Molly. They are under
weight, ailing and nearsighted. Peo-
pie endure them, and turn brightly
to the older sisters.


But Ralph and Molly are not
lacking in perception. They see
through their family and the peo-
pie around them with savage clarity.

The ministers compromised some

Since they have yet to agree on

Angry words, some of the angriest

aligned behind the idea of central

economically in the fields of finance,
industry, transport, communication,
foreign trade, food and agriculture.


Unity was developed when the
United States. Britain and Russia ac-

Foreign Minister Bidault's proposal

are taken separately.

The Icelandic volcano, Hekla. now
has been erupting for seven months,
and the whole mountain, the slopes
of which are entirely covered with
lava, appears in the long Arctic
night as huge ball of fire, gleam-
ing over the northern glacier.


A report from Reykjavik says that
lava-which comes from two huge
craters and is running in eight
broad streams from the foot of the
volcano-has buried II square miles
of meager Icelandic pasture under a
molten blanket 100 feet thick at
certain places.


On the other hand, thousands of
acres which had been buried by
ashes from the volcano last spring
now have been cleared by the tor
rental rains which have fallen over
Southern Iceland this summer. Only
nearby mountain tops and some
ridges remain covered.

one-man runaway of the Southern

South Carolina, 1913, and rolled

ID. c. youth; Bobby Gage and Jim
Reynolds, both of Clemson.

ern Conference standings over the

Citadel, 56-7. The triumph gave

petition for the season at Chapel

One big trouble with ancient the
aters came from the weather. The
seats were in the open air. When
the weather was cold, people stayed
at home, or shivered while they
watched play.


In Italy and Greece the weather
usually was warm enough, but rain
came pouring down from time to
time. The rain might fall ~ sud-
den shower after the people were
seated. The audience could get up
and leave, but there was little pleas
ure going home in wet clothes.


Efforts were made to provide avn
ings. Stretched over as many seats
as possible, the awnings sheltered
some Of those who went to theaters,
but they were hardly enough. Often
the awnings leaked.


Theaters were given up almost
entirely in the thousand years from
the breakup Of the Roman empire
to the time of the death of Colum-
bus. Then came new and better
theaters.


italy was the chief center Of the
new type Of theater. This theater
was shaped very much like the old
Roman theater, but it was provided
with a solid roof. The actors and
the audience were protected against
rain.


Another great step forward was
in the use of better scenery.

telephone message from his sister
Mary Jane Truman, who said that
with only slight assistance Mrs
Truman left the bed and walked
about eight steps to her favorite
rocking chair beside a window in
the little home at Grandview, Mo.


Brig. Gen. Wallace Grahm, White
House physician was delighted at
the report of her progress.


Mrs. Truman suffered a relapse In
mid-May and such grave fears were
felt for her that the President flew
to Grandview and remained at her
bedside for nearly two weeks.

LONDON, Feb. 8.-The Big -Four
Deputy Foreign Ministers agreed to-
day that the Allies should withdraw
all their troops from Austria within
80 days after treaty OF independ-
ence is signed with that country.


The agreement also accepted the
principle that control authority over
Austria should end when the treaty
comes into force, British sources re-
ported.


The deputies considered also an
American proposal to give small ma
tions a bigger voice in drafting rec
concentrations for the German and
Austrian peace treaties.


Some OF these nations have de-
manded that they be allowed full
participation in the work of the
Deputies, making drafts for their
chiefs, who will meet in Moscow,
March 10. The American proposal
would meet them part way on this
demand.


Presented yesterday by Robert
Murphy, the American plan would
give the little nations four seats on
the deputies committees, let active
wartime belligerents among them
give their views in committee, and
invite competent German author
tiles and experts" likewise to present
their views.

Saturday night costume ball. An
other 80 persons were in hospitals.


Capt. Frank Walten, British fire
chief, said he did not expect the
death toll to climb much higher.


A check Of British rosters showed
seven soldiers missing, the British
provost marshal's Office said. Four
British soldiers were hospitalized
with burns.


Meanwhile, German authorities
were attempting to identify the
bodies. Only three Of the 81 have
so far been identified, they said.


Stoves or Wiring Blamed.


Various causes were advanced for
the holocaust-likened to the dis
astrous Cocoanut Grove blaze In
Boston four years ago, which caused
492 deaths. A British fire control
officer blamed overheated stoves,
while a German civilian, familiar
with the structure, said short cir
cult caused the fire. The German
recalled that the flames first broke
out in the ceiling and the lights
went out Immediately.


An Army announcement said
three British soldiers were found
among the charred bodies.


Eyewitnesses told a macobre story
of glilling crowds trying to force
their way out of the flaming ball
room and hopelessly jamming the
exits, of others who needlessly sac
rificed their lives by returning to
look for their coats.


1T was the most terrible thing
I've ever seen," said Reginald Pres
ton, British soldier who was near
the main exit when the blaze broke
out.


Suddenly somebody screamed
and when looked up I saw fire
spreading along a ledge above the
ballroom pillars. Then quickly the
whole ballroom seemed to be afire.

bars in front and I couldn't get out. |

downward and I dashed to side
door What struck me then was

to be moving. but standing there

Several women who fell were

were standing there were naked be-
cause their clothes were torn off in

German fire trucks, but their COM
bined efforts were not enough to

Have you ever visited a chocolate
factory? Well, it is an experience
that should never be overlooked.


The story of the chocolate bar
really starts in the faraway coun-
tries that produce cacao beans,
These beans are dried and packed
in their native countries, then
shipped throughout the world. The
United States consumes nearly half
of the worlds cacao output.


When the beans are received at
the factory, they are cleaned and
roasted until their shells become
brittle. The shells are removed,
leaving what is called the nib"
The nibs are ground until they be-
come liquid chocolate. Large por-
tions of sugar and milk are mixed
into huge pots of this bubbling sirup.


From these large pots, the sirup
is poured into large pans. or molds
The molds then enter a cooling
chamber in which the chocolate
hardens within half-hour.


The chocolate continues its jour-
ney to the knockout" department,
where the molds are emptied. A
piece of cardboard is placed over
the pans, and the mold and card
board alike are tipped over and
gently Knocked" against a board
releasing the hard chocolate onto
the cardboard


Millions of labels and wrappers
are produced each day in the fac
tory's printing department. Special
machines are used to print with the
aluminium ink used on the wrappers
The raising of the letters also re-
quires special machines.


In the wrapping rooms, the boxes
are put together; the candy bars
are wrapped and put into the boxes
the boxes are sealed, ready for dis
tribution throughout the United
States.


Besides the manufacturing and
printing departments, the factory
which 1 visited is equipped with sep
arate lunch rooms for men and
women, lockers for every one of the
employees and emergency and first
aid rooms.

80 Planes Talked Down"

approach path, correcting deviations

a matter of seconds.


Disadvantages of the system from
the CAAs point of view are the
cost and number of men required,
the ground clutter" which shows
up on scopes located near big cities,
and the fact that the range may be
limited by electrical storms or heavy
snow at times when the sets may be
most urgently needed.

Maryland and Virginia firemen
and volunteers, wearied by two days
OF field and forest blazes, today con-
tinued on the alert for new OUT
breaks.


The latest series Of fires burned
out an estimated 5000 acres In
Maryland, the most of the damage
occurring in an area between Wash
ington and Baltimore. Six dwellings
at Texas, Baltimore County, were
burned yesterday leaving 13 families
homeless.


Montgomery and Prince Georges
County fire companies were kept
on the run all day yesterday. Near
by Virginia areas were not hit as
hard although more than 100 forest,

thousands OF acres and caused un-

900 cavalrymen and military police

broke out around 10 am.


Fire companies from most town

Howard and Prince Georges Coun-
ties, two companies from Washing

Chief John H. OLexy, Jessups

cigarette smokers.


Fort Meade Safe.


The scorched area almost sur

point flames crossed into an outly-

military installation itself was not
endangered, however.


+. j. Dalstrom, superintendent of
supply for the District Fire Depart
ment, toured the Maryland fire
area throughout the day.


Bringing the flames under control
was made difficult by shifting
clouds of smoke caused by high
winds. This made it hard to deter
mine exactly where new outbreaks
were occurring, firemen said. An
other difficulty was the scarcity of
water.


Chief OLexey said that even
though most emergency calls were
being put through. the telephone
strike delayed many calls for fre-

Two Youths Injured.


In the fire at Texas, near Balti-

second floor of one of the burning

lands East, Indies Army, but those

vancing against the Republic of
Indonesia report their dispatches

trarily.

words had been inserted which
changed its meaning.


Acting Governor General Hubertus
van Nook announced at the begin
ming of Dutch military operations
last Monday that censorship was
being imposed only on dispatches
containing military information and
when it was lifted yesterday said its
purpose had been to keep the In
donesian forces from learning the
names of captured towns which
would indicate the location of Dutch
troops.


While the Batavia censorship was
In effect at the local cable office,
newsmen agree, its application was
generally fair according to DR.. van
Mook's specifications. Only military
information not contained in Dutch
communicates was deleted.


Censorship of pictures from the
fighting zones, however, was more
severe.

0oUsIN JACKS pasty, the one-course, din

In the mining districts of Pennsylvania and

The pasty was born of necessity in the

the mining villages of Cornwall had the

Cousin Jenny, wife of Cousin Jack, as
the Cornish miners were called, brought
this unique repast to America. Cornish
men focked here by the hundreds shortly
after the Civil War when Pennsylvania
big anthracite boom was at its height.
They brought their wives with them and
their wives brought their recipes. Cornish

enjoyed so back home When Cousin Jack

in-the-hand fare.

the first shafts in the newly opened mines
in the Upper Peninsula.

Housewives soon will feel the eff
feet Of q Is per cent increase in
wholesale food prices registered
throughout the Nation during the
week ending July 5.


The Bureau of Labor Statistics
said the general upswing was due
primarily to higher prices brought
by dairy products. eggs and fresh
fruits and vegetables. Dairy foods
during the week brought wholesale
price boosts of 81 per cent, while
fruits and vegetables went up more
than 2 per cent. the bureau said.


Milk prices rose in accordance
with new market agreements, &C
cording to the bureau. Reasons for
other increases were seasonal short
ages in the case OF butter and
cheese, and stronger consumer de-
mand and Government buying for
export in the case Of eggs.


Food prices generally showed 3

month and a 35.9 per cent increase
over the same date for the previous
year.

The Washington Hockey Lions
are back home after a brief, and dis
appointing, out-of-town fling over
the week end. They take on the
Hershey Bears, last years champs,
at Uline Arena tonight at $3.50,
hoping that a return to more famil-
lar surroundings will mean return
to the winning form displayed last
week


The Bears again are on top Of
the American Leagues Eastern di-
vision after slow start this season
and will be favored tonight. The
Lions and Bears have split in two
previous games.


Herb Lovett, 20-year-old winger
acquired by Washington from the
Chicago Blackhawks, may make his
local debut tonight, but latest word
on injured Scotty Mair, another
winger, is that he has resumed
skating but probably won't return
to action until Friday.


Three of the key players who have
sparked Hershey's recent comeback
are Gordie Bruce, Penti Lund and
Bobby Schnurr, all forwards and all
from the Boston Olympics team of
last year. Goalie Gordon (Red)
Henry also has shown tighter play
in the Hershey nets recently and
something of duel is expected be-
tween him and the fast WASHINGTON
forward lines.

DAVENPORT, Iowa, Nov. 8.-One
child was killed and nine persons,
including six children, were injured
last night when an explosion de-
molished two apartments near the
edge of the city's business district


Two of the nine victims in Mercy
Hospital were in critical condition
suffering from burns and cuts.


The explosion, which police said
was caused by gas leak from an
undisclosed source, wrecked the two
CT the row of apartments half
block long on Warren street. The
blast was felt throughout the busi-
ness district of this East Central
Iowa community of 10000 and de-
bris was tossed for nearly half
block.

FORT ROBINSON, Nebr. - Old
Indian-fighters won't believe it until
the last soldier shoulders his pack
and hikes away.


But the word from Washington
Is that old Fort Robinson is being
shifted from the War Department
to the Agriculture Department.


It's a sad change to contemplate
for a proud frontier outpost which
played a great part in the winning
of the West"


For tale-spinning oldtimers among
the Indians and early settlers. it's
the body blow after the forts World
War II assignment: Training dogs


Of course, they were war dogs
taught to be as ruthless with the
enemy as was Chief Crazy Horse
who first broke Clusters line at the
Little Big Horn.


Still, they were just dogs. Not
regiments of stout young men put
ting down the greatest uprising in
Indian history.


Built in 1874.


Only a year after it was built in
1874, the fort was sending out
columns to fight the Cheyennes and
the Sioux. The campaign lasted
three years, with no clear decision
on either side.


It was during this three-year
war that Crazy Horse and Chief
Sitting Bull led the slaughter of
Custer and his men. When Crazy
Horse finally was taken, he met
death inside Fort Robinson's gates.


Crazy Horse died in the same
gua-dhouse from which Chief Dull
Knife and his band made dra-
matte escape. Dull Knife and his
men were killed-but not until their
bravery and chivalry toward their
women and children had won them
great admiration.


Gold was discovered in the nearby
Black Hills of South Dakota. Some
of the flood Of immigrants refused
to honor the lines between Indian
and Yankee country. Fort Robin
son troops were kept busy protect
ing American prospectors, even
those who trespassed on Indian do
main.


Old Settlers Remember.


There are no more Indian wars
But there are wrinkled old Indians

ported cases to 60 down steadily.

cases reported during the last week
in August. Twenty other States

ISTANBUL, Sept. 16.-President
Ismet Inonu says that Turkey re-

he said grew violent at times-to
bring her into World War II against
Soviet Russia.


In lengthy article written for the
Encyclopaedia Britapnica at Chi
cago and distributed by the official
Anatolla Agency today, Mr.. Inonu
defended Turkeys war role which
often had been criticized because
Turkey swung over to the side of
the Allies only few weeks before
Germany surrendered.


Germany, Mr.. Inonu said, spared
no effort to bring Turkey into the
conflict.


"One OF the most important events
for Turkey came when Germany
started her most threatening politi-
cal aggression" Mr.. Inonu wrote.
During Frances occupation docu-
ments had fallen into German hands
and in virtue of these it was pro-
claimed that the Turks had been
partisans of certain Anglo-French
projects against the Russians.


Germans Worked for Conflict.


"In publishing the French docu-
ments the Germans worked with all
their heart to provoke in this
troubled tense atmosphere an armed
conflict between the Russians and
Turks. Also they presumed the
Turks-left alone-would approach
them as did the Romanians, in order
to guarantee themselves against
Russian aggression"


MIR. Inonu said Turkey rejected
fatty all German demands for pas
sage toward the mideast while the
Reich armies were assaulting Egypt.
turkey had a treaty of alliance with
Britain which was defending Africa
and in 1910 Mr.. Inonu told the Ma

to say that the bonds of alliance
between Turkey and Britain are
firm and unbreakable at this mo-
ment when the British are fighting
heroically a war of existence under
difficult conditions"


Turkey massed her armies in
Thrace and Izmir, Mr.. Inonu said,
expecting momentarily that her
turn would come after the Balkan
invasion, but unexpectedly relations
between the Soviets and Bulgaria
took on new aspect and there were
occasions of demonstrations against
the Turks"


Attack on Turks Indicated.


"In short everything indicated an
attack was being prepared against

WOODWARD, Okla. April 12.--
Relatives today were completing ar
.rangements for the burial of the 81
victims Of the tornado here Wednes-
day night which left 1000 injured
and caused property damage esti-
mated In the millions.


The Northwestern Oklahamo City
was hardest hit of the Texas and
Oklahoma communities in the path
of the storm. More than SO other
persons were killed or died ofsirl-

INJURIES taxed hospital facilitate.


Higgins, Tex. listed 80 dead and
Glazier, Tex, IA. There were
dead in Gage, Okla. Total casual
ties in the twister which first struck
in the Northern Texas panhandle
and swept northeastward into Okla
homa were 140 dead and an esti-
mated 1905 injured. Work crews
searched for other victims.


Donations OF money, clothing and
food poured into Higgins and Gla-
zier. A fund to rebuild the shat
tered towns reached $4,000 in
Amarillo.


Plans for mass funeral services
in Woodward have been abandoned.
Insetad, four of the leading
churches have arranged separate
rites, the first to be held today for
Is victims.


The Rev. D. Allen Pollen, Method
list pastor, said his church would
begin funeral services tomorrow
morning, continuing them on an
hourly schedule throughout the day.


Yesterday relatives stood in line at


the city clerks office to procure


burial lots in the city cemetery.

burials probably will continue


through next week.


The bodies Of four victims, all
children ranging in age from 9
months to 6 years, remain uniden-
titled.


Even as the community went
about the sorrowing task of burying
| It's dead, its leaders laid long-range
plans for reconstruction.


City Commissioners George Trego
and Jack Courtney, Mayor r. A.
Bosch and city businessmen were
assured in a meeting last night with
housing officials from Oklahoma
City, Amarillo and Dallas that
building materials for immediate
needs would be diverted to the area.
